C H A P T E R 2

# Hull Structures and Arrangements

S E C T I O N 1 2

# Machinery Space and Tunnel

## 1 General

## 1.1 Objective (2024)

1.1.1 Goals

The vessel structure is to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goal</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact conditions, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT 5.1</td><td>Design and construct vessel, machinery, and electrical systems to facilitate safe access, ease of inspection, survey, and maintenance..</td></tr></table>

The goals in the cross-referenced Rules are also to be met.

## 1.1.2 Functional Requirements

To achieve the above stated goals, the design, construction, installation, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>Scantlings are to have sufficient strength to resist failure and excessive deformation associated with buckling and yielding when subjected to the loads anticipated throughout the service life, including hydrostatic loads (tank and watertight boundaries), load from machinery and shafting, etc.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>Suitable tightness of tanks and decks are to be provided.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>The design of the termination of structural members is to prevent yielding or fatigue cracks.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR4</td><td>Scantlings are to be maintained so that the structure will continue to satisfy all Goals and Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR5</td><td>Bolted connections are to be designed to properly transmit load between structural elements.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR6</td><td>The foundations for main propulsion units, reduction gears, shaft and thrust bearings, and the structure supporting those foundations are to be adequate in strength and rigidity, to maintain required alignment under all anticipated conditions of loading.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR7</td><td>All parts of the machinery, shafting, etc. are to be efficiently supported and the adjacent structure is to be adequately stiffened.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Safety Management (MGMT)</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT-FR1</td><td>Satisfactory arrangements are to be provided for safe access for operation, inspection and maintenance</td></tr></table>

The goals and functional requirements in cross-referenced Rules are to be met.

## 1.1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved, refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 1.3 Arrangement (2024)

In view of the effect upon the structure of the necessary openings in the machinery space, the difficulty of securing adequate support for the decks, of maintaining the stiffness of sides and bottom and of distributing the weight of the machinery, special attention is directed to the need for arranging, in the early stages of design, for the provision of plated through beams and such casing and pillar supports as are required to secure structural efficiency. Careful attention to these features in design and construction is to be regarded as of the utmost importance.

i) All parts of the machinery, shafting, etc., are to be efficiently supported and the adjacent structure is to be adequately stiffened.

ii) In twin-screw vessels it is necessary to make additions to the strength of the structure and the area of attachments, in proportion to the weight, power and dimensions of the machinery, especially where engines are relatively high in proportion to the width of the bed plate.

iii) The height and approximate weight of engines are to be stated upon the bolting plan, which is to be approved before the bottom construction is commenced. The foundations for main propulsion units, reduction gears, shaft and thrust bearings, and the structure supporting those foundations to be adequate in strength and rigidity, to maintain required alignment under all anticipated conditions of loading.

iv) The foundations and their supporting structures are to be to satisfaction of each manufacturer for main propulsion units, reduction gears, and thrust bearings. (See 4-3-2/7.3).

## 1.5 Testing of Tunnels

Requirements for testing are contained in Part 3, Chapter 7.

## 3 Machinery Foundations

## 3.1 Engine Foundations

## 3.1.1 Single Bottom Vessels

In vessels with single bottoms, the engines are to be seated on thick plates laid across the top of deep floors or upon heavy foundation girders efficiently bracketed and stiffened. Intercostal plates are to be fitted between the floors beneath the lines of bolting to distribute the weight effectively through the bottom structure to the shell. Seat plates are to be of thickness and width appropriate to the holding-down bolts and are to be effectively attached to girders and intercostals.

## 3.1.2 Double Bottom Vessels (2024)

In vessels with double bottoms, the engines are to be seated directly upon thick inner-bottom plating or upon thick seat plates on top of heavy foundations arranged to distribute the weight effectively. The thickness of the inner bottom plating is to be at least 19.0 mm (0.75 in.) in way of engine bed plates or thrust blocks which are bolted directly to the inner bottom. This thickness may be required to be increased according to the size and power of the engine(s). Holding-down bolts are to pass through angle flanges of sufficient breadth to take the nuts.

Additional intercostal girders are to be fitted within the double bottom, to provide satisfactory distribution of the weight and the rigidity of the structure.

For vessels of less than 90 meters (295 feet) in length, inner-bottom plating thickness is to be sufficient against the worst case scenario of the anticipated loads and vibrations.

## 3.3 Boiler Foundations (2024)

Boilers, if provided, are to be supported by deep saddle-type floors or by transverse or fore-and-aft girders arranged to distribute the weight effectively. Where they are supported by transverse saddles or girders, the floors in way of boilers are to be suitably increased in thickness and specially stiffened (refer to 3-2-4/5). Boilers are to be installed such as to provide accessibility and proper ventilation being clear of tank tops, bunker walls, etc., as required by 4-4-1/19.3. The thickness of adjacent material is to be increased where the clear space is unavoidably sparse. The available clearance is to be indicated on the plans submitted for approval.

## Commentary:

The requirement for bottom clearance under boilers is applicable to those boilers which are installed on the engine room floors or inner bottom plates and not applicable if the boiler is located on tween decks in machinery spaces.

The required increase of adjacent material (e.g., double bottom structures) where the clear space is unavoidably sparse is, in general, 1.5 mm (0.06 in.) in thickness in light of the effect of heat corrosion.

Thickness increase of the plating is not necessary if the bottom of the furnace is well insulated and no heat radiates to the structural member

## End of Commentary

## 3.5 Thrust Foundations (2024)

Thrust blocks are to be bolted to efficient foundations extending well beyond the thrust blocks and arranged to distribute the loads effectively into the adjacent structure. The thickness of the inner bottom plating in way of thrust blocks which are bolted directly to the inner bottom is to be as required by [3.1.2] .

## Commentary:

Consideration should be given to fitting effectively attached extra intercostal girders in way ofthe foundations to the satisfaction of each manufacturer.

End of Commentary

## 3.7 Shaft Bearing and Auxiliary Machinery Foundations

Foundations of the shaft bearings are to be strong, stiff and integrated into surrounding structure. Auxiliary machinery foundations are to be proportioned to the weight supported.

## 5 Tunnels and Tunnel Recesses

## 5.1 Plating (2024)

The plating of flat sides of shaft or other watertight tunnels is to be of the thickness as obtained from 3-2-9/5.1 for watertight bulkheads; but the lowest strake of the plating is to be increased 1 mm (0.04 in.). Flat plating on the tops of tunnels or tunnel recesses is to be of the thickness required for watertight bulkhead plating at the same level, where unsheathed in way of hatches, the thickness is to be increased 2 mm (0.08 in.).

Where the top of the tunnel or recess forms a part of a deck, the thickness is to be not less than required for the plating of watertight bulkheads at the same level plus 1 mm (0.04 in.) nor less than would be required for the deck plating in the same location.

Curved plating may be of the thickness required for watertight bulkhead plating at the same level in association using stiffener spacing of 150 mm (6 in.) less than actually adopted. Crown plating in way of hatches is to be increased at least 2.5 mm (0.10 in.) or is to be protected by wood sheathing of not less than 50 mm (2 in.) thick.

## 5.3 Stiffeners (2024)

Stiffeners are not to be spaced more than 915 mm (36 in.) apart and each stiffener, in association with the plating to which it is attached, is to have a section modulus SM not less than obtained from the following equation:

cm<sup>3</sup>

$$
S M = 0. 0 0 2 3 h s \ell^ {2} \mathrm{in} ^ {3}
$$

where

h = distance, in m (ft), from the middle of to the bulkhead deck at center

= spacing of stiffeners, in m (ft)

l = distance, in m (ft), between the top and bottom supporting members without brackets

The ends of stiffeners are to be welded to the top and bottom supporting members. Where masts, stanchions, etc., are supported by tunnels, local strengthening is to be provided proportional to the weight carried.

## 5.5 Beams, Pillars and Girders

Beams, pillars and girders under the tops of tunnels, or tunnel recesses are to be as required for similar members on bulkhead recesses.

## 5.7 Tunnels Through Deep Tanks

Where tunnels pass through deep tanks, the thickness of the plating and the size of the stiffeners in way of the tanks is not to be less than required for deep-tank bulkheads. Tunnels of circular form are to have plating of not less thickness t than obtained from the following equation:

t = 0.1345dh + 9 mm

t = 0.000492dh + 0.36 in.

where

d = diameter of the tunnel, in m (ft)

h = distance, in m (ft), from the bottom of the tunnel to the highest point of the following:

● the load line

the highest level to which the tank contents may rise in service conditions

a point located at a distance two-thirds D, as defined in 3-1-1/7.1, above the baseline

a point located two-thirds of the test head above the top of the tank

S E C T I O N 1 3

# Stems, Stern Frames, Rudder Horns, and Propeller Nozzles

## 1 General (2024)

## 1.1 Objective

1.1.1 Goals

The vessel structure is to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goal</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact condition, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr><tr><td>MAT 2</td><td>The manufacturing process is to be capable of producing products to meet the specified quality and property requirements.</td></tr><tr><td>MAT 3</td><td>The fabrication and welding process is to be capable of producing products that meets the specified quality and property requirements.</td></tr></table>

The goals in the cross-referenced Rules are also to be met.

## 1.1.2 Functional Requirements

To achieve the above stated goals, the design, construction, installation, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>Scantlings are to have sufficient strength to resist failure and excessive deformation associated with buckling and yielding when subjected to the loads anticipated throughoutthe service life, including bow impact load, slamming load, hydrodynamic lift and drag loads, vibration, load from rudders, propellers, and propulsion improvement devices.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>The design of the termination of structural members is to be such as to prevent yielding or fatigue cracks.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>The workmanship is to avoid discontinuities, misalignment and other harmful details that may lead to failure in service.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR4</td><td>Scantlings are to be maintained so that the structure will continue to satisfy all Goals and Functional Requirements throughout the expected service life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR5</td><td>Sufficient structural strength is to be provided to resist cracking, buckling, fatigue damage, deformation, erosion due to cavitation, corrosion, or vibration from propeller forces which would impair the structural integrity of the ship.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR6</td><td>The foundations and the supporting structures for shaft and propulsion improvement devices are to be adequate in strength and rigidity.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR7</td><td>Fabrication is to be of sufficient quality (welding, structural tolerances, alignment, defects) so that the finished product performs in accordance with the design assumptions.</td></tr></table>

The goals and functional requirements in cross-referenced Rules are to be met.

## 1.1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved. Refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 2 Stems

Depending on size and design of the vessel stems may be made of bent and welded steel plates, of formed cast or forged steel, or of steel bar.

## 2.1 Plate Stems (2024)

Plate stems, where used, are not to be less in thickness than required by the following equations, in the draft change zone (between the minimum draft and the maximum draft). See [FIGURE 1A] .

$$
\begin{array}{l l l l} t & = & 1. 5 + (L / 1 2) \sqrt {q} \mathrm{mm} & L \leq 2 4 5 \mathrm{m} \\ t & = & 1. 5 + 2 0. 5 \sqrt {q} \mathrm{mm} & 2 4 5 <   L \leq 3 0 5 \mathrm{m} \\ t & = & 0. 0 6 + (L / 1 0 0 0) \sqrt {q} \text {in}. & L \leq 8 0 0 \mathrm{ft} \\ t & = & 0. 0 6 + 0. 8 \sqrt {q} \text {in}. & 8 0 0 <   L \leq 1 0 0 0 \mathrm{ft} \end{array}
$$

where

q N/mm<sup>2</sup> ( kgf/mm<sup>2</sup> , psi)

Y = specified minimum yield point or yield strength, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>,psi), as defined in [2-1-1/13] of the ABS Rulesfor Materials and Welding (Part 2), for the higher-strength material or 72% of the specified minimum tensile strength, whichever is the lesser.

L = length of vessel, as defined in 3-1-1/3.1, in m (ft)

Above and below the draft change zone, the thickness may taper to the thickness of the shell at ends at the freeboard deck and to the thickness of the flat-plate keel at the forefoot, respectively.

## 2.3 Cast or Forged Stems (2024)

Cast or forged stems as shown in [FIGURE 1B] of special shape are to be proportioned to provide strength at least equivalent to that of a plate stem, and all joints and connections are to be at least that effective.

## 2.5 Bar Stems (2024)

Bar stems as shown in [FIGURE 1C] are to have thickness and width not less than obtained from the following equations:

t = 0.625L + 6.35 mm

$$
t = 0. 0 0 7 5 L + 0. 2 5 \mathrm{in}.
$$

$$
w = 1. 2 5 L + 9 0 \mathrm{mm}
$$

$$
w = 0. 0 1 5 L + 3. 5 \mathrm{in}.
$$

where

t = thickness, in mm (in.)

w = width, in mm (in.)

L = length of vessel, in m (ft), as defined in 3-1-1/3.1

## Commentary:

In general, the thickness of the bar stem should also not be less than twice the adjoining shell thickness.

## End of Commentary

This thickness and width is to be maintained between the keel and scantling draft line. Above the scantling draft line they may be gradually reduced until the section area at the freeboard deck is 0.7 of that obtained from the above equations.

Thicknesses and widths other than given above are acceptable, provided the section moduli and moments of inertia about the longitudinal axis are not less than calculated from above, nor is proportion of w/t more than 5.5.

## 3 Stern Frames (2024)

Stern frames may be fabricated from steel plates or made of cast steel. For applicable material specifications and steel grades, see 3-1-2/1.3.1 and 3-1-2/3.1 TABLE 2A. The scantlings are to comply with [3.3] and [3.5] .

Cast stern frames and shoe pieces are to be manufactured from special grade material per [2-1-5/7.3] .

Commentary:

Stern frames of other material or construction may be specially considered by ABS. Consideration should be given to provide measures against cavitation erosion.

End of Commentary

## 3.1 Rudder Gudgeons (2024)

Rudder gudgeons are to be an integral part of the stern frame. The bearing length of the pintle is to be between 1.0 and 1.2 times the pintle diameter (refer to 3-2-14/13.7). The thickness of the pintle housing is not to be less than 25% of the pintle diameter. See the figure below:

## 3.5 Stern Frames with Shoe Piece

The scantlings below the boss of stern frames with shoe pieces are to be gradually increased to provide strength and stiffness in proportion to those of shoe pieces.

## 3.7 Scantlings Above the Propeller Boss

Above the propeller boss, the scantlings are to be in accordance with [3.3] except that in the upper part of the propeller aperture, where the hull form is full and centerline supports are provided, the thickness may be reduced to 0.8 of the requirements in [3.3] , subject to the same minimum for a cast steel stern frame.

## 3.9 Secondary Members

Where round bars are used at the after edge of stern frames, their scantlings and connection details are to be such as will accomplish acceptable welding.

Ribs or horizontal brackets of thickness not less than 0.8 t or $0 . 8 ~ t _ { 1 }$ are to be provided at suitable intervals. Where t or $t _ { 1 }$ is reduced in accordance with [3.7] , a proportionate reduction in the thickness of ribs or horizontal brackets may be made.

## 3.11 Shoe Pieces (2024)

The shoe-piece is to be sloped to avoid pressure from the keel blocks when docking and is to extend at least two frame spaces forward of the forward edge of the propeller boss.

The equivalent stress $\sigma _ { e }$ in the shoe piece at any section is not to exceed $1 1 5 / K _ { g } \mathrm { N / m m } ^ { 2 } ( 1 1 . 7 / K _ { g } \mathrm { k g f / m m } ^ { 2 } )$ $1 6 7 0 0 / K _ { g }$ psi) and is to be obtained from the following equation:

$$
\sigma_ {e} = n \sqrt {\sigma_ {b} ^ {2} + 3 \tau^ {2}} \mathrm{N/mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{kgf/mm} ^ {2}, \mathrm{lbs/in} ^ {2}) (\mathrm{psi})
$$

where

n = 1000 (1000, 2240)

$K _ { g }$ = shoe-piece material factor as defined in 3-2-14/1.5

$\sigma _ { b }$ = bending stress =

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force, as defined in 3-2-14/3

2 = horizontal distance between centerline of rudder stock and the section of the stern frame shoe piece under consideration, in m (in.) (see [FIGURE 2])

$Z _ { v }$ = section modulus of shoe piece about the vertical axis at the particular section under consideration, in cm<sup>3</sup> (in<sup>3</sup>)

τ = shear stress $= 0 . 5 C _ { R } / A _ { s }$

$A _ { s }$ = effective shear area in the transverse direction at the section of the shoe piece under consideration in, mm<sup>2</sup> (in<sup>2</sup>)

In addition, shoe piece width is to be approximately twice the depth, and vertical and horizontal section modulus and sectional area are in no case to be less than required by the following equations.

$$
{Z _ {z}} = {k _ {z} C _ {R} \ell K _ {g}} {\mathrm{cm} ^ {3} (\mathrm{in} ^ {3})}
$$

$$
Z _ {y} = 0. 5 Z _ {z} \mathrm{cm} ^ {3} (\mathrm{in} ^ {3})
$$

$$
{A _ {s}} = {k _ {a} C _ {R} K _ {g}} {\mathrm{mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{in} ^ {2})}
$$

where

$Z _ { z }$ = minimum required section modulus of shoe piece about the vertical axis at the particular section under consideration

$Z _ { y }$ = minimum required section modulus of shoe piece about the transverse horizontal axis at the particular section under consideration

$A _ { s }$ effective shear area in the transverse direction at the section of the shoe piece under consideration, in $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } )$

$k _ { z }$ = 6.25 (61.3, 0.0967)

$k _ { a }$ = 10.4 (102, 0.161)

## 5 Rudder Horns

## 5.1 Scantlings - Single Pintle Rudders

The strength of the rudder horn is to be based on the most critical location at any point up to and in way of the connection into the hull. At no section is the equivalent stress $\sigma _ { e }$ in the rudder horn to exceed $1 2 0 / K _ { h }$ N/ mm<sup>2</sup> (12.2/K<sub>h</sub> kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 17400/K<sub>h</sub> lbs/in<sup>2</sup>) where $\sigma _ { e }$ is obtained from the following equation:

$$
\sigma_ {e} = n \sqrt {\sigma_ {b} ^ {2} + 3 (\tau^ {2} + \tau_ {T} ^ {2})} \mathrm{N/mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{kgf/mm} ^ {2}, \mathrm{lbs/in} ^ {2})
$$

where

n = 1000 (1000, 2240)

$\sigma _ { b }$ bending stress =

$\tau$ = shear stress due to bending =

$\tau _ { T }$ = shear stress due to torque $= 0 . 5 C _ { R } \ell _ { a } \ell _ { h } / ( \ell _ { p } a t )$

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force, as defined in 3-2-14/3

$\ell _ { a }$ = vertical distance, in m (ft), from the center of the neck bearing to the centroid of A (see [FIGURE 3] a)

$\ell _ { p }$ = vertical distance, in m (ft), from the center of the neck bearing to the center of the pintle bearing (see [FIGURE 3] a)

$\ell _ { v }$ = vertical distance, in m (in.), from the center of the pintle bearing to the section of the rudder horn being considered (see [FIGURE 3] a)

$\ell _ { h }$ = horizontal distance in, mm (in.), from the center of the pintle bearing to the center of area of the horizontal plane of the rudder horn at the section of the rudder horn being considered (see [FIGURE 3] a)

section modulus of the rudder horn about the longitudinal axis, in $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 3 } )$ , at the section of the rudder horn $S M$ = being considered

$A _ { h }$ effective shear area of the rudder horn in the transverse direction at the section being considered, in mm $^ { 2 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } )$

area, in $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } )$ , enclosed by the outside lines of the rudder horn at the section of the rudder horn being $a$ = considered

t = minimum wall thickness of the rudder horn, in mm (in.), at the section being considered

$K _ { h }$ = rudder horn material factor as defined in 3-2-14/1.5

$K _ { h }$ as defined in 3-2-14/1.5 for castings and forgings

= 1.0 for ordinary strength hull steel plate

= $Q$ as defined in 3-2-1/5.3 for higher strength steel plate

In addition to meeting the above maximum equivalent stress criteria, the shear stress is not to be greater than indicated in the following equation.

$$
\tau = 4 8 / K _ {h} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2} \left(4. 9 / K _ {h} \mathrm{kgf} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2}, 6 9 6 0 / K _ {h} \mathrm{lbs} / \mathrm{in} ^ {2}\right)
$$

Also, the section modulus about the longitudinal horizontal axis is not to be less than given in the following equation:

$$
S M = n _ {z} C _ {R} (\ell_ {a} / \ell_ {p}) \ell_ {v} K _ {h} \mathbf {c m} ^ {3} (\mathbf {i n} ^ {3})
$$

$$
n _ {z} = 1 4. 9 (1 4 6. 4, 0. 2 3 0)
$$

Webs extending down into the horn as far as practicable are to be fitted and effectively connected to the plate floors in the after peak. At the shell, the change in section of the horn is to be as gradual as possible. Smooth curvature or radii are to be provided at abrupt changes of section where stress concentrations occur.

## 5.3 Scantlings - Two Pintle Rudders

The strength of the rudder horn is to meet the requirements for single pintle horns given in [5.1] above, with the following modified definitions of lever arm and component stresses.

$\ell _ { a }$ vertical distance, in m (ft), from the center of the upper pintle to the centroid of A (see [FIGURE 3] b)

$\ell _ { p }$ = vertical distance, in m (ft), from the center of the upper pintle bearing to the center of the lower pintle bearing (see [FIGURE 3] b)

$\ell _ { v }$ = vertical distance, in m (in.), from the center of the lower pintle bearing to the section of the rudder horn being considered up to the entry of the horn into the shell plating (see [FIGURE 3] b)

$\ell _ { h }$ = horizontal distance, in mm (in.), from the center of the lower gudgeon to the center of area of the horizontal plane of the rudder horn at the section of the rudder horn being considered (see [FIGURE 3] b)

$\sigma _ { b }$ bending stress

= $C _ { R } \ell _ { a } \ell _ { v } / ( \ell _ { p } S M )$

between the upper and lower pintle gudgeons

= $C _ { R } ( \ell _ { v } + \ell _ { a } { - } \ell _ { p } ) / S M$

in SI or MKS units, above the upper pintle gudgeon

$C _ { R } \left[ \ell _ { v } + 1 2 ( \ell _ { a } - \ell _ { p } ) \right] / S M$

in U.S. units, above the upper pintle gudgeon

$\tau$ = shear stress due to bending $= C _ { R } \ell _ { a } / ( \ell _ { p } A _ { h } )$ between the upper and lower pintle gudgeons

= $C _ { R } / A _ { h }$ above the upper gudgeon

$\tau _ { T }$ = shear stress due to torque $= 0 . 5 C _ { R } \ell _ { a } \ell _ { h } / ( \ell _ { p } a t )$ between the upper and lower pintle gudgeons

= $0 . 5 C _ { R } \ell _ { h } / ( a t )$ above the upper gudgeon

## 5.4 Rudder Horn Castings (2024)

Cast rudder horns are to be manufactured from special grade material according to [2-1-5/7.3] .

## 5.5 Rudder Horn Plating (2024)

The thickness of the rudder horn side plating is not to be less than:

$t = 2 . 4 \sqrt { L k }$ mm

t = 0.522√Lk in.

Where

= length of vessel, as defined in 3-1-1/3.1;

k = as defined in 3-2-14/1.5 for castings

= 1.0 for ordinary strength hull steel plate

= as defined in 3-2-1/5.3 for higher strength steel plate

## 5.7 Welding and Connection to Hull Structure

The following requirements are to apply:

i) The rudder horn plating is to be effectively connected to the aft ship structure (e.g., by connecting the plating to side shell and transverse/longitudinal girders) in order to achieve a proper transmission of forces, see [FIGURE 4] . When the connection between the rudder horn and the hull structure is designed as a curved transition into the hull plating, special consideration should be given to the effectiveness of the rudder horn plate in bending and to the stresses in the transverse web plates

ii) Where the rudder horn does not have curved transitions into the shell plating, brackets or stringer are to be fitted internally in horn, in line with outside shell plate, as shown in [FIGURE 4] .

iii) Transverse webs ofthe rudder horn are to be led into the hull up to the next deck or flat in a sufficient number.

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$t = 0.094(L - 16) + 0.009\mathrm{smm}$ $\mathrm{for}90 &lt;   L\leq 427\mathrm{m}$ $t = 0.00113(L - 53) + 0.009\sin .$ $\mathrm{for}295 &lt;   L\leq 1400\mathrm{ft}$
</div>

iv) Strengthened plate floors are to be fitted in line with the transverse webs in order to achieve a sufficient connection with the hull.

v) Where a centerline bulkhead (wash-bulkhead) is fitted in the after peak, it is to be connected to the rudder horn.

vi) Scallops are to be avoided in way of the connection between shell plating and transverse webs in line with the aft face of the rudder horn and the webs in the rudder horn

vii) The weld at the connection between the rudder horn plating and the side shell is to be full penetration. The welding radius is to be as large as practicable and may be obtained by grinding.

## 5.9 Floors (2024)

Heavy plate floors are to be fitted both in way of the after face of the horn and aligned with the webs required by [5.1] and [5.3] . They are to be carried up to the first deck or flat above, if possible.

t = 0.035L + 8.5 mm

t = 0.0042L + 0.33 in

where

= thickness of the heavy plate floors, in mm (in)

= length of the vessel, as defined in 3-1-1/3.1, in m (ft)

## Commentary:

Heavy plate floors should extend up to the first deck or flat above, if possible.

End of Commentary

## 5.11 Shell Plating (2024)

Heavy shell plates are to be fitted in way of the heavy plate floors required by [5.9] .

The thickness of the heavy shell plates is not to be less than:

For OSVs and other Vessels under 90 m (295 ft) in Length:

## 5.13 Water Exclusion

Rudder horns are to be provided with means for draining water, except where rudder horns are filled with an approved waterproof material, or equivalent.

## 7 Shaft Struts

Tail-shaft (propeller-shaft) struts, where provided, may be of the V or I type. The thickness of the strut barrel or boss is to be at least one-fourth the diameter of the tail shaft. The length of the strut barrel or boss is to be adequate to accommodate the required length of propeller-end bearings. The following equations are for struts having streamlined cross-sectional shapes.

## 7.1 V Strut (2024)

The moment of inertia, , and Section Modulus, , of each strut arm is not to be less than that obtained from the following equations:

$$
I = 0. 0 0 4 4 d ^ {4} \mathrm{mm} ^ {4} (\mathrm{in} ^ {4})
$$

$$
S M = 0. 0 2 4 d ^ {3} \mathrm{mm} ^ {3} (\mathrm{in} ^ {3})
$$

where

d = required diameter of ABS Grade 2 tail shaft, in mm (in.)

Commentary:

Where the included angle is less than 45°, the foregoing scantlings should be specially considered.

End of Commentary

## 7.3 I Strut

The moment of inertia, , and Section Modulus, , of the strut arm is not to be less than that obtained from the following equations:

$$
I = 0. 0 1 8 d ^ {4} \mathrm{mm} ^ {4} (\mathrm{in} ^ {4})
$$

$$
S M = 0. 0 6 8 d ^ {3} \mathrm{mm} ^ {3} (\mathrm{in} ^ {3})
$$

where

d = required diameter of ABS Grade 2 tail shaft, in mm (in.)

![](ABS-Rules_for_Building_and_Classing_Marine_Vessels%E2%80%94Part3-Hull_Construction_and_Equipment/part-0201-0400/images/22d738d937851bb358d55e0a92d85c01dd38e521223bd276e0811e0c150b999c.jpg)

## 7.5 Strut Length

The length of the longer leg of a V strut or the leg of an I strut, measured from the outside perimeter of the strut barrel or boss to the outside of the shell plating, is not to exceed 10.6 times the diameter of the tail shaft. Where this length is exceeded, the width and thickness of the strut are to be increased, and the strut design will be given special consideration.

## Propeller Nozzles (2024)

The requirements in this Subsection are applicable for propeller nozzles with inner diameter of 5 meters (16.4 feet) or less.

## Commentary:

Nozzles with larger inner diameters are subject to special consideration by ABS, and all supporting documents and calculations should be submitted for review.

## End of Commentary

## 9.7 Welding Requirement (2024)

The inner and outer nozzle shell plating is to be welded to the internal stiffening ring webs with double continuous welds except the outer shell plating when inaccessible for welding. Plug/slot welding is prohibited for the inner shell, but may be acceptable for the outer shell plating, provided that the nozzle ring web spacing is not greater than 350 mm (13.8 in.).

## 11 Propulsion Improvement Devices (PID) (1 July 2025)

## 11.1 Application Scope (1 July 2025)

The requirements in this Subsection are applicable to the connection of the Propulsion Improvement Devices (PID) to the hull. Types of PIDs include wake equalizing and flow separation alleviating devices (such as spoilers, wake equalizer, stern tunnels, pre-swirl fins, stators, and pre-swirl ducts) and post swirl devices (such as rudder thrust fins, post swirl stators, and rudder bulbs) that are permanently affixed to the hull structure.

## 11.3 Plans and Documentation (1 July 2025)

The following plans and details are to be submitted for approval, while the calculations are to be submitted for reference:

i) Drawings and plans covering the detailed design of the end connections and attachment to the hull structure;

ii) Information on material properties and welding details, such as scantlings of the welded connection and welding detail and size;

iii) Calculations to validate the design of the supporting foundations interior to the vessel.

## 11.5 Design and Arrangement (1 July 2025)

The following requirements are to be complied with for the types of propulsion improvement devices outlined in [11.1] :

## Commentary:

Devices of novel concept may be specially considered by ABS. All related drawings and documents should be submitted.

## End of Commentary

i) The structural materials are to be compatible with the mechanical and chemical properties of the hull strake to which it is attached. Examples of such design considerations are to have adequate structural strength for load bearing/transferring and acceptable galvanic potential between materials to reduce the risk of galvanic corrosion.

ii) PID end connections are to have a suitable transition for the particular application and to be effectively terminated in way of internal stiffening members.

iii) The strength and fatigue of the connection of the PID to the hull are to be within the limits of these Rules or other acceptable standards when subjected to vibration, hydrodynamic lift and drag loads in both the ahead and astern conditions. Certain types of PID (such as rudder bulbs or other such design elements) need only be checked for strength.

## 11.7 Structural End Connection

Welded end connections of device structural component to the hull are to be designed and constructed in accordance with the following:

i) Welding at the connection is to be full penetration and is to be in accordance with [2-4-1] of the ABS Rulesfor Materials and Welding (Part 2) and Section 3-2-19, as applicable

ii) Nondestructive volumetric and surface examinations are to be performed on the welds of the connection plates and the shell penetration. 100% Magnetic Testing (MT) and at least 10% Ultrasonic Testing (UT) is to be carried out on the welds of the connection plates and the shell penetration.

## 13 Inspection of Castings (2025)

The location of radiographic or other subsurface inspections of large stern-frame and rudder-horn castings is to be in accordance with [2-1-5/13.11] and Part 2, Appendix 6 and indicated on inspection plans, and to be agreed with the attending Surveyor.

Hull Structures and Arrangements

S E C T I O N 1 4

# Rudders and Steering Equipment

## 1 General

## 1.1 Objective (2024)

1.1.1 Goals

The vessel structures covered in this section are to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goal</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact condition, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr><tr><td>MAT 1</td><td>The selected materials&#x27; physical, mechanical, and chemical properties are to meet the design requirements appropriate for the application, operating conditions, and environment.</td></tr><tr><td>PROP 4</td><td>Provide means to maneuver the vessel.</td></tr><tr><td>PROP 5</td><td>Provide redundancy and/or reliability to maintain maneuverability.</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT 5.1</td><td>Design and construct vessel, machinery, and electrical systems to facilitate safe access, ease of inspection, survey, and maintenance.</td></tr></table>

## 1.1.2 Functional Requirements

To achieve the above stated goals, the design, construction, installation, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>Scantlings are to have sufficient strength to resist failure and excessive deformation associated with buckling and yielding when subjected to the loads anticipated throughoutthe service life, such as external sea loads, operational loads in ahead/astern conditions and vibration.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>Scantlings are to be maintained so that the structure will continue to satisfy all Goals and Functional Requirements.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>The termination of structural members is to be designed to avoid stress concentrations that may lead to yielding or fatigue cracks.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR4</td><td>Welded connections are to have sufficient strength to resist failure and fatigue damage.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR5</td><td>The workmanship is to avoid discontinuities, misalignment and other harmful details that may lead to failure in service.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR6</td><td>Protective devices to avoid exceeding operational limitations is to be provided</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR7</td><td>Effective locking of parts that may come loose due to vibration and/or dynamic loads is to be provided.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Materials (MAT)</td></tr><tr><td>MAT-FR1</td><td>Materials are to have corrosion and wear resistance appropriate for the operating environment and service life.</td></tr><tr><td>MAT-FR2</td><td>Galvanic corrosion due to dissimilar materials is to be avoided.</td></tr><tr><td>MAT-FR3</td><td>Welded connections are to be free from defects and discontinuities.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Safety Management (MGMT)</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT-FR1</td><td>Satisfactory arrangements are to be provided for safe access for operation, inspection, and maintenance.</td></tr></table>

## 1.1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved. Refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 1.3 Application (2024)

Requirements specified in this Section are applicable to:

## 1.3.1

Ordinary profile rudders described in [TABLE 1A] with rudder operating angle range from –35° to +35°.

## 1.3.2

High-lift rudders described in [TABLE 1B] , the rudder operating angle of which might exceed 35° on each side at maximum design speed.

## 1.3.3 (2024)

Steering equipment other than rudders, such as steering nozzles, azimuthal thruster and azimuthing pod identified in [21] , [23] , and [25] , respectively.

Rudders and other steering equipment provided on Ice Classed vessels are subject to additional requirements specified in Part 6, Chapter 1 for the specified ice class.

Commentary:

Rudders not covered in [TABLE 1A] nor in [TABLE 1B] are subject to special consideration, provided that all the required calculations are prepared and submitted for review in full compliance with the requirements in this Section. Where direct analyses is used to justify an alternative design, they are to take into consideration all relevant modes of failure, on a case-bycase basis. These failure modes may include yielding, fatigue, buckling, and fracture. Possible damages caused by cavitation and vibration are also to be considered. Validation by laboratory tests or full scale tests may be required for alternative design approaches.

The IACS Technical Background file for UR S10 may be referred to for more information.

## End of Commentary

## 1.5 Materials for Rudder, Rudder Stock and Steering Equipment

Rudder stocks, pintles, coupling bolts, keys and other steering equipment components described in this Section are to be of steel, in accordance with the requirements of Part 2, Chapter 1, 3-1-2/3.1 TABLE 2A and 3-1-2/3.1 TABLE 2B, and particularly:

i) The Surveyor need not witness material tests for coupling bolts and keys.

ii) The surfaces of rudder stocks in way of exposed bearings are to be of noncorrosive material.

iii) Material properties of dissimilar parts and components in direct contact with each other are to be submitted for review of compatibilities, such as galvanic potential.

iv) Material factors of castings and forgings used for the shoe piece $( K _ { g } )$ , horn $( K _ { h } )$ , stock $( K _ { s } )$ , bolts $( K _ { b } )$ , coupling flange $( K _ { f } )$ , pintles $( K _ { p } )$ , and nozzles $\left( K _ { n } \right)$ are to be obtained for their respective material from the following equation:

$$
K = (n _ {y} / Y) ^ {e}
$$

where

$n _ { y }$ = 235 N/mm<sup>2</sup> (24 kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 34000 psi)

$Y$ = specified minimum yield strength of the material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi), but is not to be taken as greater than or 450 N/mm<sup>2</sup> (46 kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 65000 psi) whichever is less

= minimum tensile strength of material used, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

e 二 1.0 for N/mm<sup>2</sup> (24 kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 34000 psi)

= $0 . 7 5$ for $Y >$ N/mm<sup>2</sup> (24 kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 34000 psi)

## 1.7 Expected Torque (2024)

The torque considered necessary to operate the rudder, in accordance with 4-3-4/21.7.ii.) is to be indicated on the submitted rudder or steering gear plan (see 4-3-4/1.11).

## Commentary:

Note that the above expected operating torque is not the design torque, $Q _ { R }$ , indicated in [5.3] for rudder scantlings. The design torque is intended for the design of rudders and should not be directly compared with the torque expected during th sea trials or the rated torque of steering gear (see 4-3-4/1.11).

## End of Commentary

## 1.9 Rudder Stops

Structural rudder stops are to be fitted. Each structural stop as well as its attachment is to withstand the rudder design force applied at stop’s location. Where adequate positive mechanical stops are provided within the steering gear in accordance with 4-3-4/5.11, structural stops are not required.

## 3 Rudder Design Force (2022)

Rudder force, $C _ { R } ,$ , upon which rudder scantlings are to be based, is to be obtained from the equation described either in [3.1] or [3.3] as applicable. For vessels under 90 meters (295 feet) in length, where for ordinary rudders the rudder angle, , exceeds 35°, the rudder force, $C _ { R }$ , is to be increased by a factor of 1.74 sin ( ).

## 3.1 Rudder Blades without Cutouts (1 July 2024)

Where the rudder profile can be defined by a single quadrilateral, the rudder force, $C _ { R }$ , upon which rudder scantlings are to be based, is to be obtained from the following equation:

$C _ { R } = n k _ { R } k _ { c } k _ { \ell } A V _ { R } ^ { 2 }$ kN (tf, Ltf)

where

$$
n \quad = 0. 1 3 2 (0. 0 1 3 5, 0. 0 0 1 2 3)
$$

$k _ { R }$ = $( b ^ { 2 } / A _ { t } + 2 ) / 3$ but not taken more than 1.33

$b$ = mean height of rudder area, in m (ft), as determined from [FIGURE 1A]

$A _ { t }$ = sum of rudder blade area, $A ,$ and the area of rudder post or rudder horn within the extension of rudder profile, in $\mathbf { m } ^ { 2 } \left( \mathbf { f } \mathbf { t } ^ { 2 } \right)$

$A$ = total projected area of rudder blade, as illustrated in [FIGURE 1A] in $\mathbf { m } ^ { 2 } \left( \mathbf { f } \mathbf { t } ^ { 2 } \right)$ For steering nozzles, is not to be taken less than 1.35 times the projected area of the nozzle.

$k _ { c }$ = coefficient depending on rudder cross section (profile type) as indicated in [TABLE 1A] and [TABLE 1B] . For profile types differing from those in [TABLE 1A] and [TABLE 1B] , $k _ { c }$ is subject to special consideration.

$k _ { \ell }$ = coefficient as specified in [TABLE 2]

$V _ { R }$ = vessel speed, in knots

= for ahead condition $V _ { R }$ equals $V _ { d }$ or $V _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ , whichever is greater

= for astern condition $V _ { R }$ equals $V _ { a }$ , or $0 . 5 V _ { d }$ or $0 . 5 V _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ , whichever is greater

$V _ { d }$ = design speed, in knots, with vessel running ahead at the maximum continuous rated shaft rpm and at the summer load waterline

$V _ { a }$ = maximum astern speed as defined in SOLAS Regulation II-1/3.15, in knots

$V _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ = (Vd + 20)/3

Where there are any appendages such as rudder bulb fitted on the rudder, its effective areas are to be included in the area of the rudder blade if significant.

## 3.3 Rudder Blades with Cutouts

This paragraph applies to rudders with cutouts (semi-spade rudders), such that the whole blade area cannot be adequately defined by a single quadrilateral. See [FIGURE 1B] . Equations derived in this paragraph are based on a cutout blade with two quadrilaterals. Where more quadrilaterals are needed to define the rudder shape, similar rules apply.

The total rudder force described in [3.1] is applicable for rudders with cutout(s), with being the summation of sub-quadrilaterals that make up the whole area of the rudder blade. Rudder force distribution over each quadrilateral is to be obtained from the following equations:

$$
C _ {R 1} = C _ {R} A _ {1} / A \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

kN (tf, Ltf)

where

$C _ { R }$ and are as defined in [3.1] .

$A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 2 }$ are as described in [FIGURE 1B] .

## 3.5 Rudder Blades with Twisted Leading-edge (2024)

This kind of rudder has the leading edge twisted horizontally on the top and bottom of the section that is an extension of the center of the propeller shaft. For the purpose of calculating design force, twisted rudders are distinguished in four categories:

<table><tr><td>Category</td><td>Description</td></tr><tr><td>1</td><td>The leading edge of twisted upper and lower blades not lineup to each other (See 3-2-14/Figure 1(a) below)</td></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>The projected leading edge of twisted upper and lower blades form a straight line (See 3-2-14/Figure 1(b) below)</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>Rudder with twisted leading-edge combined with tail edge flap or fins</td></tr><tr><td>4</td><td>The twisted leading edge has a smooth continuous wavy contour (no deflector) (See 3-2-14/Figure 1(c) below) or the rudder has multiple section profile types</td></tr></table>

FIGURE 1 Rudder Blades with Twisted Leading-edge (2024)  
![](ABS-Rules_for_Building_and_Classing_Marine_Vessels%E2%80%94Part3-Hull_Construction_and_Equipment/part-0201-0400/images/2501a2474a5ff11b45bbd455965466b765ceff76e2c36f34bfc6e304ab725a21.jpg)

Design force for rudder with twisted leading edge is obtained according to the following criteria:

i) For Category 1 rudders as indicated in the above table, design force over upper and lower rudder blades are obtained from the following equations respectively:

$$
C _ {R 1} = n k _ {R} k _ {c} k _ {\ell} A _ {1} V _ {R} ^ {2}
$$

kN (tf, Ltf) for twisted upper rudder blade;

$$
C _ {R 2} = n k _ {R} k _ {c} k _ {\ell} A _ {2} V _ {R} ^ {2}
$$

kN (tf, Ltf) for twisted lower rudder blade;

$$
C _ {R} = C _ {R 1} + C _ {R 2}
$$

kN (tf, Ltf) overall design force;

ii) For Categories 2, 3, and 4, the rudder design force indicated in [3.1] is applicable, that is: $C _ { R } = n k _ { R } k _ { c } k _ { \ell } A V _ { R } ^ { 2 }$ kN (tf, Ltf)

where

n, kR, $k _ { c } , k _ { \ell } , A$ and $V _ { R }$ are as defined in [3.1] , (for rudder has multiple section profile types, is the whole projected areas).

$A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 2 }$ are the projected areas of upper and lower blades separated at the deflector cross section, respectively. Where the effective projected area ofrudder bulb (ifpresent) forward ofrudder leading edge is significant and needs to be counted, the proportioned bulb effective areas are added to and $A _ { 2 }$ accordingly

Values of $k _ { c }$ for ahead and astern conditions are determined from one of the methods below as applicable, if the type of basic rudder profile is not provided:

a) $k _ { c }$ is taken from [TABLE 1A] for twisted rudders of Categories 1 & 2;

b) $k _ { c }$ is taken from [TABLE 1B] for twisted rudders of Category 3;

c) $k _ { c }$ is subjected to special considerations for twisted rudders of Category 4;

Commentary:

Shipyard/rudder manufacturers’ submitted $k _ { c }$ obtained from testing data or calculations may be accepted subject to ABS review of all the supporting documents;

End of Commentary

## 5 Rudder Design Torque (2024)

## 5.1 General

The rudder design torque, $Q _ { R }$ , for rudder scantling calculations, is to be in accordance with [5.3] or [5.5] as applicable.

## 5.3 Rudder Blades without Cutouts

Rudder torque, $Q _ { R } ,$ , is to be determined from the following equation for both ahead and astern conditions:

$$
Q _ {R} = C _ {R} r \mathrm{kN-m(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

where

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force as calculated in [3.1]

r = but not less than for ahead condition

c = mean breadth of rudder area as shown in [FIGURE 1A] , in m (ft)

α coefficient as indicated in [TABLE 3]

k = $A _ { f } / A$

$A _ { f }$ = area of rudder blade situated forward of the rudder stock centerline, in m<sup>2</sup> (ft<sup>2</sup>), as shown in [FIGURE 1A]

$A$ = whole rudder area as described in [3.1]

Where there are any appendages such as rudder bulb fitted on the rudder, effective areas are to be included in the area of the rudder blade if significant.

## 5.5 Rudder Blades with Cutouts

This paragraph refers to rudder blades with cutouts (semi-spade rudders) as defined in [3.3] . Equations derived in this paragraph are based on a cutout blade with two quadrilaterals. Where more quadrilaterals are needed to define the rudder shape, similar rules apply.

Total rudder torque, $Q _ { R }$ , in ahead and astern conditions is to be obtained from the following equation:

$$
Q _ {R} = C _ {R 1} r _ {1} + C _ {R 2} r _ {2} \mathrm{kN-m(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

but not to be taken less than $Q _ { R \mathrm { m i n } }$ in the ahead condition

where

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$Q_{R\min}$ = $0.1C_R(A_1c_1 + A_2c_2) / A$ $r_1$ = $c_{1}(\alpha -k_{1})\mathrm{m}$ (ft.)   
$r_2$ = $c_{2}(\alpha -k_{2})\mathrm{m}$ (ft.)   
$c_{1},c_{2}$ = mean breadth of partial area $A_{1},A_{2}$ , from [FIGURE 1B]   
$\alpha$ = coefficient as indicated in [TABLE 3]   
$k_{1},k_{2}$ = $A_{1f} / A_1,A_{2f} / A_2$ where $A_{1f},A_{2f} =$ area of rudder blade situated forward of the centerline of the rudder stock for each part of the rudder, as shown in [TABLE 1B]
</div>

$C _ { R } , C _ { R 1 } , C _ { R 2 } , A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 }$ are as defined in [3.3] .

## 5.7 Rudders with Twisted Leading Edge

Rudder torque, , indicated in [5.3] is applicable for rudders with twisted leading edge, where $C _ { R }$ is obtained from [3.5] .

## 7 Rudder Stocks

## 7.1 Upper Rudder Stocks (2024)

The upper stock is that part of the rudder stock above the neck bearing or above the top pintle, as applicable. (See 3-2-A5/3 FIGURE 1, 3-2-A5/5.1 FIGURE 2 and 3 for reference.)

At the upper bearing or tiller, the upper stock diameter is not to be less than obtained from the following equation:

```javascript
[S = N _ { u } \sqrt [ 3 ] { Q _ { R } K _ { s } } \mathrm { m m } ( \mathrm { i n . } )]
```

where

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$N_{u} = 42.0(89.9,2.39)$
</div>

$Q _ { R }$ = total rudder torque, as defined in [5] , in kN-m (tf-m, Ltf-ft)

$K _ { s }$ = material factor for upper rudder stock, as defined in [1.3]

## 7.3 Lower Rudder Stocks (1 July 2024)

In determining lower rudder stock scantlings, values of rudder design force and torque calculated in [3] and [5] are to be used. Bending moments and shear forces, as well as the reaction forces are to be determined by direct calculation and are to be submitted for review. For rudders supported by shoe pieces or rudder horns, these structures are to be included in the calculation model to account for support of the rudder body. Guidance for calculation of these values is given in Appendix 3-2-A5.

The lower rudder stock diameter is not to be less than obtained from the following equation:

$$
S _ {\ell} = S \sqrt [ 6 ]{1 + (4 / 3) (M / Q _ {R}) ^ {2}} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

where

= upper stock required diameter from [7.1] , in mm (in.)

= bending moment at the section of the rudder stock considered, in kN-m (tf-m, Ltf-ft)

= rudder torque from [5] , in kN-m (tf-m, Ltf-ft)

Above the neck bearing, a gradual transition is to be provided where there is a change in the diameter of the rudder stock.

The equivalent stress of bending and torsion, to be assessed from the aforementioned direct calculation in the transition is not to exceed 118/K N/mm<sup>2</sup> (12.0/K kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 17100/K lbs/in<sup>2</sup>).

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$\sigma_{c} = \sqrt{\sigma_{b}^{2} + 3\tau^{2}}$ N/mm² (kgf/mm², lbs/in²)  
where  
$K =$ material factor as defined in [1.3]  
$\sigma_{b} = 10.2\times 10^{6}M / S_{t}^{3}$ for SI and MKS units  
$= 270\times 10^{3}M / S_{t}^{3}$ for US units  
$\tau = 5.1\times 10^{6}Q_{R} / S_{t}^{3}$ for SI and MKS units  
$= 135\times 10^{3}Q_{R} / S_{t}^{3}$ for US units
</div>

For a spade rudder with trunk extending inside the rudder, the rudder stock scantlings are to be checked against the two cases defined in 3-2-A5/3.1.3.

## 7.5 Rudder Trunk and Rudder Stock Sealing (1 July 2024)

The requirements in 3-2-14/7.5 iii), iv) and v) apply to trunk configurations which extend below the stern frame and arranged in such a way that the trunk is stressed by forces due to rudder action.

i) In rudder trunks which are open to the sea, a seal or stuffing box is to be fitted above the deepest load waterline, to prevent water from entering the steering gear compartment and the lubricant from being washed away from the rudder carrier.

ii) Where the top of the rudder trunk is below the waterline at scantling draft (without trim), two separate watertight seals/stuffing boxes are to be provided.

iii) Materials. The steel used for the rudder trunk is to be of weldable quality, with a carbon content not exceeding 0.23% on ladle analysis or a carbon equivalent (Ceq) not exceeding 0.41%. Plating materials for rudder trunks are not to be of lower grades than corresponding to class II as defined in 3-1-2/3.1 TABLE 1. Rudder trunks comprising of materials other than steel are to be specially approved.

iv) Scantlings. The scantlings of the trunk are to be such that the equivalent stress due to bending and shear does not exceed , and the bending stress on the welded rudder trunk is to be in compliance with the following formula:

For calculation of bending stress, the span to be considered is the distance between the mid-height of the lower rudder stock bearing and the point where the trunk is clamped into the shell or the bottom of the skeg.

v) Welding at the Connection to the Hull. The weld at the connection between the rudder trunk and the shell or the bottom of the skeg is to be full penetration and a fillet shoulder is to be provided in way of the weld. For rudder trunks extending below shell or skeg, the fillet shoulder radius , in mm (in.) (see [FIGURE 2] ) is to be as large as practicable and to comply with the formulae:

The radius may be obtained by grinding. If disk grinding is carried out, score marks are to be avoided in the direction of the weld. The radius is to be checked with a template for accuracy. A minimum of four profiles are to be checked. A report is to be submitted to the Surveyor.

## 9 Flange Couplings

## 9.1 General (2024)

Rudder flange couplings are to comply with the following requirements:

i) Couplings are to be supported by an ample body of metal worked out from the rudder stock. Couplings welded to the rudder stock are to be in accordance with [9.3.3] and [9.5.3] .

ii) The smallest distance from the edge of the bolt holes to the edge of the flange is not to be less than two-thirds of the bolt diameter.

iii) Coupling bolts are to be fitted bolts.

iv) Suitable means are to be provided for locking the nuts in place.

In addition to the above, rudder flange couplings are to meet the type-specific requirements in [9.3] (horizontal couplings) or [9.5] (vertical couplings) as applicable.

## 9.3 Horizontal Couplings

## 9.3.1 Coupling Bolts (2024)

There are to be at least six coupling bolts in horizontal couplings, and the diameter, , of each bolt is not to be less than obtained by the following equation:

$$
d _ {b} = 0. 6 2 \sqrt {d _ {s} ^ {3} k _ {b} / (n r K _ {s})} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

where

$d _ { s }$ required rudder stock diameter, ( [7.1] ) or ( [7.3] ) as applicable, in way of the coupling

= total number of bolts in the horizontal coupling

r mean distance of the bolt axes from the center of the bolt system, in mm (in.), (mathematical average of the bolt axes distances from the axis of the stock)

$K _ { b }$ 二 material factor for bolts, as defined in [1.3]

$K _ { s }$ = material factor for stock, as defined in [1.3]

## 9.3.2 Coupling Flange

Coupling flange thickness is not to be less than the greater of the following equations:

$$
t _ {f} = d _ {b t} \sqrt {K _ {f} / K _ {b}} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

$$
t _ {f} = 0. 9 d _ {b t} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

where

$d _ { b t }$ = calculated bolt diameter calculated as per [9.3.1] based on a number of bolts not exceeding eight (8)

$K _ { f }$ = material factor for flange, as defined in [1.3]

$K _ { b }$ = material factor of bolts, as defined in [1.3]

## 9.3.3 Joint between Rudder Stock and Coupling Flange

The welded joint between the rudder stock and the flange is to be made in accordance with [FIGURE 3] or equivalent.

## 9.5.1 Coupling Bolts

There are to be at least eight coupling bolts in vertical couplings and the diameter of each bolt is not to be less than obtained from the following equation:

$$
d _ {b} = 0. 8 1 d _ {s} \sqrt {K _ {b} / (n K _ {s})} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

where

= total number of bolts in the vertical coupling, which is not to be less than 8

$d _ { s } , K _ { b } , K _ { s }$ as defined in [9.3] .

In addition, the first moment of area, , of the bolts about the center of the coupling is not to be less than given by the following equation:

$$
m = 0. 0 0 0 4 3 d _ {s} ^ {3} \mathrm{mm} ^ {3} (\mathrm{in} ^ {3})
$$

where

$d _ { s }$ = diameter, in mm (in.), as defined in [9.3]

## 9.5.2 Coupling Flange

Coupling flange thickness, , is not to be less than as defined in [9.5.1] .

## 9.5.3 Joint between Rudder Stock and Coupling Flange

The welded joint between the rudder stock and the flange is to be made in accordance with [FIGURE 3] or equivalent.

## 11 Tapered Stock Couplings

## 11.1 Coupling Taper (1 July 2021)

Tapered stock couplings are to comply with the following general requirements in addition to type-specific requirements given in [11.3] or [11.5] as applicable:

i) Tapered stocks, as shown in [FIGURE 4] , are to be effectively secured to the rudder casting by a nut on the end.

ii) The cone shapes are to fit exactly.

iii) The coupling length ( ) in the casting as shown in [FIGURE 4A] is generally not to be less than 1.5 times the stock diameter ( ) as shown in [FIGURE 4] .

iv) The taper on diameter ( ) is to be 1/12 to 1/8 for keyed taper couplings and 1/20 to 1/12 for couplings with hydraulic mounting/dismounting arrangements, as shown in the following table. The cone length is defined in [FIGURE 4A] .

v) Where mounting with an oil injection and hydraulic nut, the push-up oil pressure and the push-up length are to be specially considered upon submission of calculations.

vi) Means of effective sealing are to be provided to protect against sea water ingress.

## 11.3 Keyed Fitting (2024)

Where the stock is keyed, the key is to be fitted in accordance with the following:

i) The top of the keyway is to be located well below the top of the rudder.

Commentary:

To achieve this requirement, sufficient material should remain between the keyway and the top ofthe rudder to avoid damage due to the accidental movement of the rudder. See [15.5] .

## End of Commentary

ii) Torsional strength of the key equivalent to that of the required upper stock is to be provided.

iii) For the couplings between stock and rudder the effective shear area\* of the key is not to be less than:

$$
a _ {s} = \frac {1 7 . 5 5 Q _ {F}}{d _ {k} \sigma_ {F 1}} \mathrm{cm} ^ {2}
$$

$$
a _ {s} = \frac {2 1 . 0 6 Q _ {F}}{d _ {k} \sigma_ {F 1}} \mathrm{in} ^ {2}
$$

where

= design yield moment of rudder stock, in N-m (kgf-m, lbf-ft)

$$
= 0. 0 2 6 6 4 \frac {d _ {t} ^ {3}}{k}
$$

$$
\mathrm{N-m}
$$

$$
= 0. 0 0 2 7 1 7 \frac {d _ {t} ^ {3}}{k}
$$

kgf-m

$$
= 3 2 1. 9 8 3 8 \frac {d _ {t} ^ {3}}{k}
$$

$$
\mathrm{lbf-ft}
$$

Where the actual rudder stock diameter $d _ { t a }$ is greater than the calculated diameter $d _ { t }$ , the diameter $d _ { t a }$ is to be used. However, $d _ { t a }$ applied to the above formula need not be taken greater than .

$d _ { t }$ = stock diameter, in mm (in.), according to [7.1]

$k$ = material factor for stock as given in [1.3]

$d _ { k }$ mean diameter of the conical part of the rudder stock, in mm (in.), at the key

= minimum yield stress of the key material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

The effective bearing area<sup>\*</sup> of the key (after deducting the rounded edges) between key and rudder stock or cone coupling is not to be less than:

$$
a _ {k} = \frac {5 Q _ {F}}{d _ {k} \sigma_ {F 2}} \mathrm{cm} ^ {2}
$$

$$
a _ {k} = \frac {6 Q _ {F}}{d _ {k} \sigma_ {F 2}} \mathrm{in} ^ {2}
$$

where

= minimum yield stress of the key, stock or coupling material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi), whichever is less.

iv) For keys of higher strength materials than that for the keyway, shear and bearing areas of keys and keyways may be based on the respective material properties of the keys and the keyways, provided that compatibilities in mechanical properties of both components are fully considered. In no case, is the bearing stress of the key on the keyway to exceed 0.9 of the specified minimum yield strength of the keyway material.

Commentary:

In general, the key material is to be at least of equal strength to the keyway material.

## End of Commentary

v) Push up. It is to be proved that 50% of the design yield moment is solely transmitted by friction in the cone couplings. This can be done by calculating the required push-up pressure and push-up length according to [11.5v.] ) and [11.5vi.]) for a torsional moment $Q _ { F } ^ { ' } = 0 . 5 Q _ { F } .$

vi) Where a key is fitted to the coupling between stock and rudder and it is considered that the entire rudder torque is transmitted by the key at the couplings, the requirement of 3-2-14/11.3v) need not be applied provided that the actual shear area and the effective surface area of the key are more than twice of that required by 3-2-14/11.3iii).

## Commentary:

\* The effective shear/bearing area is to be the gross area reduced by any area removed by saw cuts, set screw holes, chamfer, etc., and is to exclude the portion of the key in way of spooning of the keyway.

## End of Commentary

## 11.5 Keyless Fitting (1 July 2024)

Hydraulic and shrink fit keyless couplings are to be fitted in accordance with the following:

i) Detailed preloading stress calculations and fitting instructions are to be submitted;

ii) Prior to applying hydraulic pressure, at least 75% of theoretical contact area of rudder stock and rudder bore is to be achieved in an evenly distributed manner;

iii) The upper edge of the upper main piece bore is to have a slight radius;

iv) Push-up Pressure. The push-up pressure is not to be less than the greater of the two following values:

$$
p _ {r e q 1} = \frac {2 Q _ {F}}{d _ {m} ^ {2} \ell \pi \mu_ {o}} 1 0 ^ {3} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2})}
$$

$$
p _ {r e q 1} = \frac {2 4 Q _ {F}}{d _ {m} ^ {2} \ell \pi \mu_ {o}} \mathrm{psi}
$$

$$
p _ {r e q 2} = \frac {6 M _ {c}}{d _ {m} \ell^ {2}} 1 0 ^ {3} \mathrm{N/mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{kgf/mm} ^ {2})
$$

$$
p _ {r e q 2} = \frac {7 2 M _ {c}}{d _ {m} \ell^ {2}} \mathrm{psi}
$$

where

$Q _ { F }$ = design yield moment of rudder stock, as defined in [11.3iii.] )

$d _ { m }$ = mean cone diameter, in mm (in.)

l = coupling length, in mm (in.)

$\mu _ { o }$ = frictional coefficient, equal to 0.15

$M _ { c }$ = bending moment in rudder stock at the top of the cone coupling (e.g., in case of spade rudders), in N-m (kgf-m, lbf-ft)

For spade rudder with trunk extending inside the rudder, the coupling is to be checked against the two cases defined in 3-2-A5/3.1.3.

It has to be proved by the designer that the push-up pressure does not exceed the permissible surface pressure in the cone. The permissible surface pressure is to be determined by the following formula:

$$
p _ {p e r m} = \frac {0 . 9 5 Y _ {G} (1 - \alpha^ {2})}{\sqrt {3 + \alpha^ {4}}} - p _ {b} \mathrm{N/mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm {kgf / mm^ {2}}, \mathrm{psi})
$$

where

$$
{p _ {b}} = {\frac {3 . 5 M _ {c}}{d _ {m} \ell^ {2}} 1 0 ^ {3} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kg / m m ^ {2})}}
$$

pb = $\frac { 4 2 M _ { c } } { d _ { m } \ell ^ { 2 } } \mathrm { p s i }$

$Y _ { G }$ = specified minimum yield strength of the material of the gudgeon or stock, whichever is smaller, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

$\alpha$ = $d _ { m } / d _ { a }$

$d _ { m }$ = mean cone diameter, in mm (in.)

$d _ { a }$ = outer diameter of the gudgeon, in mm (in.) as shown in 3-2-14/FIGURE 4B (The least diameter is to be considered)

The outer diameter of the gudgeon in mm (in.) is not to be less than , with $d _ { 0 }$ defined in [FIGURE 4] .

FIGURE 4B

Gudgeon Outer Diameter Measurement (1 July 2021)

![](ABS-Rules_for_Building_and_Classing_Marine_Vessels%E2%80%94Part3-Hull_Construction_and_Equipment/part-0201-0400/images/f9236c56df21a9353d2464f6580d82b7e6120fee0b3428aa75e7cf491cc66c6a.jpg)

v) Push-up Length. The push-up length , in mm (in.), is to comply with the following formula: $\Delta \ell _ { 1 } \leq \Delta \ell \leq \Delta \ell _ { 2 }$

$$
\Delta \ell_ {1} = \frac {P _ {r e q} d _ {m}}{E \left(\frac {1 - \alpha^ {2}}{2}\right) c} + \frac {0 . 8 R _ {t m}}{c} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

$$
\Delta \ell_ {2} = \frac {P _ {p e r m} d _ {m}}{E \left(\frac {1 - \alpha^ {2}}{2}\right) c} + \frac {0 . 8 R _ {m}}{c} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

$R _ { t m }$ = mean roughness, in mm (in.) taken equal to 0.01 mm (0.0000394 in.)

c = taper on diameter according to [11.1iv.] )

$Y _ { G }$ = specified minimum yield strength of the material of the gudgeon, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

$E$ = Young’s modulus of the material of the gudgeon, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

$Y _ { G } , \alpha$ , and $d _ { m }$ are as defined in [11.5v.] ).

Commentary:

In case of hydraulic pressure connections the required push-up force $P _ { e }$ for the cone may be determined by the following formula:

$$
P _ {e} = p _ {r e q} d _ {m} \pi \ell \left(\frac {c}{2} + 0. 0 2\right) \mathrm{N(kgf,lbf)}
$$

The value 0.02 is a reference for the friction coefficient using oil pressure. It varies and depends on the mechanica treatment and roughness of the details to be fixed. Where due to the fitting procedure a partial push-up effect caused by the rudder weight is given, this may be taken into account when fixing the required push-up length, subject to approval.

## End of Commentary

vi) Couplings with Special Arrangements for Mounting and Dismounting the Couplings. Where the stock diameter exceeds 200 mm (8 in.), the press fit is recommended to be effected by a hydraulic pressure connection. In such cases the cone is to be more slender, to . In case of hydraulic pressure connections the nut is to be effectively secured against the rudder stock or the pintle. For the safe transmission of the torsional moment by the coupling between rudder stock and rudder body the push-up pressure and the push-up length are to be determined according to [11.5v.] ) and [11.5vi.] ), respectively.

vii) The locking nut is to be fitted in accordance with [11.7] .

## 11.7 Locking Nut (2022)

Dimensions of the securing nut, as shown in [FIGURE 4] , are to be proportioned in accordance with the following and the nut is to be fitted with an effective locking device.

Height $h _ { n } \geq 0 . 6 d _ { g }$

Outer diameter of nut $d _ { n } \ge 1 . 2 d _ { u }$ or whichever is greater

External thread diameter $d _ { g } \geq 0 . 6 5 d _ { o }$

In the case of a hydraulic pressure secured nut, a securing device such as a securing flat bar is to be provided [see [9.1iv.] ]. Calculations proving the effectiveness of the securing device are to be submitted.

A securing flat bar will be regarded as an effective securing device for the nut, if its shear area, in mm<sup>2</sup> (in<sup>2</sup>), is not less than:

$$
A _ {S} = \frac {P _ {S} \cdot \sqrt {3}}{\sigma_ {F}} \mathrm{mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{in} ^ {2})
$$

where

= shear force, in N (kgf, lbf)

$$
= \frac {P _ {e}}{2} \mu_ {1} \left(\frac {d _ {1}}{d _ {g}} - 0. 6\right)
$$

= push-up force, in N (kgf, lbf), as defined in [11.5.v.]

$\mu _ { 1 }$ = frictional coefficient between nut and rudder body, normally $\mu _ { 1 } = 0 . 3$

$d _ { 1 }$ = mean diameter of the frictional area between nut and rudder body, in mm (in.)

$d _ { g }$ = external thread diameter of the nut, in mm (in.)

$\sigma _ { F }$ specified minimum yield stress of the securing flat bar material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

## 13.3 Couplings (2024)

## 13.3.1 Tapering (2024)

Pintles assembled with use of a locking nut are to have a conical attachment to the gudgeons with a taper not greater than:

1:8 – 1:12 for keyed and other manually assembled pintles with locking nut.

1:12 – 1:20 for pintles mounted with oil injection and hydraulic nut.

## 13.3.2 Push-up Pressure (1 July 2024)

The required push-up pressure for pintles in case of dry fitting, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi), is to be determined by as given below.

The required push-up pressure for pintles in case of oil injection fitting, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi), is to be determined by the maximum pressure of and as given below.

## 13.3.3 Push-up Length (1 July 2024)

The required push-up length, $\Delta \ell _ { 1 }$ , is to be calculated similarly as in [11.5vi.] ), using the required push-up pressure as defined in 3-2-14/13.3.2 above, and properties for the pintle.

## 13.5 Threads and Nuts (2024)

Threads and nuts are to be in accordance with [11.7] .

## 13.7 Pintle Housing (2024)

## 13.7.1 Length (2024)

The length of the pintle housing in the gudgeon is not to be less than the pintle diameter, $D _ { p }$ where $D _ { p }$ is to be measured on the outside of liners.

## 13.7.2 Thickness (2024)

The thickness of the pintle housing is not to be less than 25% of the actual pintle diameter (refer 3-2-13/3.1).

## 13.9 Bearings (2024)

For rudders on horns with two pintles, as shown in 3-2-13/3.3.1 FIGURE 3b, calculations are to include pintle bearing forces with the vessel running ahead at the maximum continuous rated shaft rpm and at the lightest operating draft.

For rudders supported by a shoe piece and pintle assembled without the use of a nut (refer to 3-2-A5/5.1 FIGURE 2), a cylindrical attachment may be accepted as simply supported on the condition that the pintle bearing clearance allows enough space for angular inclination under the associated rudder design force.

The bearing pressure is to be in accordance with [15.1] .

Special consideration is to be given to metal bearings and unique rudder types.

Inspection plates are to be provided for the examination of pintles and securing arrangements unless alternate means, such as an inspection port, are provided.

## 15 Supporting and Anti-Lifting Arrangements

## 15.1 Rudder Stock Bearing, Rudder Shaft Bearing, and Pintle Bearing (2024)

Bearing surfaces for rudder stocks, shafts and pintles are to meet the following requirements:

## 15.1.1 Bearing Surfaces (2024)

The projected area of the bearing surface $\left( \mathbf { \nabla } A _ { b } = d _ { \ell } \boldsymbol { \ell } _ { b } \right)$ is not to be less than $A _ { b \operatorname* { m i n } }$ (see [FIGURE 4C] ).

where

$d _ { \ell }$ = outer diameter of the liner, in mm (in.)

$\ell _ { b }$ = bearing length, in mm (in.)

$$
A _ {b \mathrm{min}} = k _ {1} \frac {P}{p _ {a}} \mathrm{mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{in} ^ {2})
$$

$$
k _ {1} = 1 0 0 0 (2 2 4 0)
$$

$P$ = bearing reaction force, in kN (tf, Ltf), as specified in [TABLE 5]

$p _ { a }$ = allowable surface pressure as indicated in [TABLE 6] depending on bearing material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, psi)

## 15.1.2 Bearing Dimensions (2024)

The length/diameter ratio $\left( { \ell _ { b } } / d _ { \ell } \right)$ of the projected area of bearing surface is not to be greater than 1.2\*:

The bearing length $L _ { p }$ of the pintle, in mm $( \mathrm { i n . } ) _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , is to be such that:

$$
D _ {p} \leq L _ {p} \leq 1. 2 D _ {p}
$$

where

$D _ { p }$ actual pintle diameter, in mm (in.), measured on the outside of liners

Note: \* Request for bearing arrangement of length/diameter ratio greater than 1.2 is subject to special consideration provided that calculations are submitted to show acceptable clearance at both ends of the bearing.

![](ABS-Rules_for_Building_and_Classing_Marine_Vessels%E2%80%94Part3-Hull_Construction_and_Equipment/part-0201-0400/images/26c82b6ded804deba8948fb931b96a46eddd487e415816ccf6609ef647f41a61.jpg)

## 15.1.3 Bearing Clearance

i) The clearance for metal bearings is not to be less than $d _ { i } / 1 0 0 0 + 1 . 0$ mm $( d _ { i } / 1 0 0 0 + 0 . 0 4 ~ \mathrm { { i n . } ) }$ on the diameter, where $d _ { i }$ is the inner diameter of the bushing, in mm (in.).

ii) The clearance for non-metallic bearings is to be specially determined considering the material’s swelling and thermal expansion properties. This clearance in general is not to be taken less than 1.5 mm (0.06 in.) on diameter\*.

Note: \* Request of clearance less than 1.5 mm (0.06 in.) for non-metallic bearings is subject to special considerations provided that documented evidence, such as manufacturer's recommendation on acceptable clearance, expansion allowance and satisfactory service history with reduced clearances, are submitted for review.

## 15.1.4 Bearing Pressure

Bearing pressure is to be accordance with [TABLE 6] , as applicable.

## 15.1.5 Bearing Material

Where stainless steel or wear-resistant steel is used for liners or bearings, the material properties including chemical composition of both components are to be submitted for review for an approved combination.

## 15.1.6 Liners and Bushes (1 July 2024)

i) Rudder Stock Bearings. Liners and bushes are to be fitted in way of bearings. For rudder stocks and pintles having diameter less than 200 mm (7.87 in.), provision of liners in way of bushes is optional. If a liner is not provided, the rudder stock diameter is to be increased 7 mm (0.28 in.). The minimum thickness of liners and bushes is to be equal to:

$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = 8$ mm (0.31 in.) for metallic materials and synthetic material

$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = 2 2$ mm (0.87 in.) for lignum material

## ii) Pintle Bearings

The thickness of any liner or bush is neither to be less than:

$t = k _ { 1 } \sqrt { B }$ mm (in.)

where

= bearing force, in N (kgf, lbf)

$k _ { 1 }$ 0.01 (0.0313, 0.000830)

nor than the minimum thickness defined in [15.1.5i.] )

Bearings are to be restrained from turning by keying or similar arrangements.

If the Class Notation UWILD is requested, means and access are to be provided to determine the condition and clearance of the rudder bearing, in accordance with [7-A1-1/3.5.2] .

## Commentary:

The use of resin chock material to position pintle and neck bearings may be considered acceptable subject to the following:

i The maximum bearing pressure must not exceed manufacturer's specification, or the values for maximum permissible bearing stress for rudder neck bearing and pintle bushings as provided in the ABS Rules.

ii Installation must comply with manufacturer's recommendations.

iii Details of proposed installation is to be submitted for approval. Vertical movement of the resin chock is to be prevented. Rotating stoppers are also to be provided for resin chock (axial grooves may be permitted for this purpose).

## End of Commentary

## 15.3 Rudder Carrier

i) The weight of the rudder assembly is to be supported by a rudder carrier mounted on the hull structure designed for that purpose.

ii) At least half of the rudder carrier’s holding-down bolts are to be fitted bolts. Alternative means of preventing horizontal movement of the rudder carrier may be considered.

iii) The bearing part is to be well lubricated by dripping oil, automatic grease feeding, or a similar method.

iv) Hull structures in way of the rudder carrier are to be suitably strengthened.

## 15.5 Anti-Lifting Devices

Means are to be provided to prevent accidental unshipping or undue movement of the rudder which may cause damage to the steering gear. There are to be at least two bolts in the joint of the anti-lifting ring.

## 17 Double Plate Rudder

## 17.1 Strength

Rudder section modulus and web area are to be such that stresses indicated in the following Subparagraphs are not exceeded.

In calculating the section modulus ofthe rudder, the effective width ofside plating is to be taken as not greater than twice the extreme athwartship dimension of the rudder in way of horizontal section being considered. Bolted cover plates on access or inspection openings to pintles or nuts are not to be considered effective in determining the section modulus of the rudder. For a cover plate to be considered effective, it is to be closed using a full penetration weld and confirmed suitable by non-destructive testing method. Smooth curvature or radii are to be provided at abrupt changes in section where stress concentrations occur, including in way of openings and cover plates.

Moments, shear forces and reaction forces are to be obtained by direct calculation, which is to be submitted. Guidance for calculation of these values is given in Appendix 3-2-A5.

## 17.1.1 Spade Rudders and Rudders with Horns (2024)

For spade rudders and rudders with horns, the section modulus at the bottom of the rudder is not to be less than one-third the required section modulus of the rudder at the top of the rudder or at the center of the lowest pintle.

Special attention is to be paid in design and construction of rudders with slender foil sections in the vicinity of their trailing edge (e.g., hollow foil sections, fishtail foil sections). Where the width of the rudder blade at the aftermost vertical diaphragm, , is equal or less than <sup>1</sup>/ of the trailing edge length measured between the diaphragm and the trailing edge, , finite element vibration analysis and trailing edge vortex shedding analysis of the rudder blade are also to be submitted for review. See 3-2-14/Figure 5

t _ {e} = 4 3 \alpha^ {- 0. 3 6} c _ {t} ^ {0. 5} - 3. 5 c _ {t} \mathbf {m m}
