# Calculation of Shear Stresses for Vessels Having Longitudinal Bulkheads

## 1 General (2024)

## 1.1 Objective (2024)

The objective of this section is to provide a procedure for calculation of shear stresses for vessels having longitudinal bulkheads.

## 1.2 Methods of Calculation (2024)

The nominal total shear stress in the side shell or longitudinal bulkhead plating is related to the shear flow at that point, by the following equation:

= N/t, kN/cm<sup>2</sup> (tf/cm<sup>2</sup>, Ltf/in<sup>2</sup>)

= shear flow, kN/cm (tf/cm, Ltf/in.)

t = thickness of the plating, cm (in.)

## Commentary:

Refer to Appendix [5A-5-A1] and Appendix 5C-11-A1 for guidance on calculating shear flow and shear stresses for vessels having longitudinal bulkheads.

ABS HGSA Software is available to assist in this calculation.

In calculating the shear stress for vessels having plane plate longitudinal bulkheads, for a section with openings symmetrica or unsymmetrical, or openings on only one side of the vessel, the shear flow may need to be adjusted to consider the following factors:

Size of the opening – Extent in longitudinal and vertical direction

è Extent of continuity of the longitudinal bulkhead in which the opening is located

Connectivity of the structural members/availability of nearby bulkheads for the shear to flow through/other structura members around (bulkheads to decks or flats/arrangement of the structural members in the vicinity of the opening)

Completeness of the complex girder system formed by the structural members around the opening in the section under consideration

Structural details in way of the openings such as corner radius, proposed reinforcement in way of the openings, etc., against the effects of stress concentration

A 2D full section or 3D model of a sufficient length may be required to calculate the actual shear flow and justify the shear stress in way of the section.

End of Commentary

## 3 Calculation of the Shear Flow Around Closed Sections

The shear flow of a closed and prismatic structure is expressed by the following equation.

$$
N = (F m / I) + N _ {i}, \mathrm{kN/cm(tf/cm,Ltf/in.)}
$$

$F$ = total shear force at the section under consideration, in kN(tf, Ltf)

m = first moment about the neutral axis of the section, in ${ \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 3 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 3 } ) .$ , of the area of the longitudinal material between the zero shear level and the vertical level, at which the shear stress is being calculated

m = $\int _ { o } ^ { p } { Z t d s } + \sum _ { i = o } ^ { n } { a _ { i } z _ { i } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 3 } ) }$

I = moment of inertia of the section, in $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 4 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 4 } )$

$N _ { i }$ = constant shear flow around the cell regarded as an integration constant of unknown value arising from substituting the statically indeterminate structure by statically determinate one, in kN/cm (tf/cm, Ltf/in)

$Z$ = distance from section neutral axis to a point in the girth, positive downward, in cm(in.)

a = equivalent sectional area of the stiffener or girder attached to the deck, shell and bulkhead plating, in $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } )$

S = length along girth and longitudinal bulkhead, in cm (in.)

## 5 Calculation of

To calculate the value of requires the knowledge or assumption of a zero shear point in the closed cell. As an example, in the case of a simplified tanker section, the deck point at the centerline is a known point of zero shear in the absence of the centerline girder. An arbitrary point may be chosen in the wing tank cell. Superposition of the constant $N _ { i }$ to the shear flow resulting from the assumption of zero shear point will yield to the correct shear flow around the wing cell.

## 7 Determination of

$N _ { i }$ is determined by using Bredt's torsion formula, making use of the assumption that there is no twist in the cell section, i.e., the twist moment resulting from the shear flow around a closed cell should equal zero, or $\oint N { \frac { d s } { t } } = 0$ . In a multicell structure of number of cells, the formula can be written for the $i ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ cell as follows.

$$
\oint N \frac {d s}{t} = \frac {F}{I} \oint^ {i} m _ {i} \frac {d s}{t} + N _ {i - 1} \int^ {D i v} \frac {d s}{t} + N _ {i} \oint \frac {d s}{t} + N _ {i + 1} \int^ {D i v} \frac {d s}{t} = 0
$$

Div = common division between cell and the adjacent cells and $i + 1$

The first term represents twist moment around cell at the assumed statically determined status. The values are calculated upon arbitrary zero shear points in the cell and the adjacent cells. The remaining terms in the equations represent the balancing twist moments around cell and of those carried out by the common divisions in the adjacent cells and .

To determine the constant shear flow in the cells $N _ { 1 } , \ N _ { 2 } , \ . \ . \ N _ { i } , N _ { n } , n$ number of similar equations are formed for each cell and are solved simultaneously.

# Loading Manuals and Loading Instruments

## 1 Objective (2024)

## 1.1 Goal

The vessels covered in this section are to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goals</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact condition, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr></table>

## 1.2 Functional Requirements

To achieve the above stated goals, the design, construction, installation, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>The loading conditions are to be properly defined to cover the critical cases for the intended service with the calculated still water bending moment and shear force to ensure sufficient hull girder longitudinal strength.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>Information is to be provided to enable to the vessel to operate within the designed limits of hull girder longitudinal strength, local strength of forward bottom structures against slamming, cargo hold tank tops, decks and hatch covers, designed maximum cargo density, and other designed limits and loading instructions, where applicable.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>Means is to be provided to enable the Master to quickly perform calculations to ensure the intended loading conditions meeting the designed limits of hull girder strength and local strength, where applicable.</td></tr></table>

## 1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved. Refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 2 General

## 2.1 Application (2024)

The requirements in this Appendix apply to all classed cargo vessels 65 m (213 ft) and above in length.

Additional requirements in Appendix 3-2-A3 are applied to bulk carriers, ore carriers and combination carriers having a freeboard length $\left( \begin{array} { l } { L _ { f } } \end{array} \right)$ of 150 m (492 ft) and above. $L _ { f }$ is as defined in 3-1-1/3.1.

Commentary:

These requirements satisfy Regulation 10(1) of the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 and are applicable for vessels with freeboard length, $L _ { f }$ of 65 meters (213 feet) and above.

End of Commentary

## 3 Definitions

## 3.1 Loading Guidance

Loading guidance is a generic term covering both loading manual and loading instrument, as defined below.

## 3.1.1 Loading Manual

A loading manual is a document containing sufficient information to assist the master of the vessel to arrange for the loading and ballasting of the vessel in such a way as to avoid the creation of any unacceptable stresses in the vessel’s structure.

## 3.1.2 Loading Instrument

A loading instrument is an instrument designed to assess vessel’s still water bending moments, shear forces and, where applicable, the still water torsional moments and lateral loads at the specified points along the length for the purpose not to exceed the specified values in any loaded or ballast condition.

## 3.3 Category I Vessels

Category I vessels are any of the following:

i) Vessels with large deck openings where combined stresses due to vertical and horizontal hull girder bending, torsional and lateral loads need be considered, such as container carriers.

ii) Vessels designed for non-homogeneous loading where the cargo and/or ballast may be unevenly distributed, except those belonging to [3.5.iii.] . Examples of such vessel are bulk carriers, ore carriers and combination carriers.

iii) Vessels, such as oil carriers and fuel carriers, except those belonging to [3.5.iii.] .

iv) Chemical carriers and gas carriers

## 3.5 Category II Vessels

Category II vessels are any of the following:

i) Vessels with such arrangements that only allow a small possibility for variation in cargo and ballast distribution, such as passenger ships.

ii) Vessels on regular and fixed trading pattern where the loading manual gives sufficient guidance, such as ro-ro ferries.

iii) Vessels less than 120 m (394 ft) in length, L, when their design takes into account the uneven distribution of cargo or ballast.

## 5 Loading Documents

## 5.1 Loading Manual (2024)

All vessels are to be provided with a loading manual reviewed and stamped by ABS in accordance with [7] , except for Category II vessels with length less than 90 m and the deadweight not exceeding 30% of the displacement at the summer load line.

## 5.3 Modifications

Where modifications to the vessel or to the loading/trading pattern result in changes to the input information, a revised or new loading manual is to be submitted and a stamped copy is to be placed aboard the vessel to replace the existing manual. The loading instrument is to be verified in accordance with [9.3] or newly installed and verified in such cases.

Where changes due to modification of the vessel are such that the still water bending moments and shear forces corresponding to the new loading conditions are within ±2% of the existing allowable values, the existing allowable values need not be modified.

## 7 Loading Manual

## 7.1 Required Information

The loading manual is to be based on the final data of the vessel and is to include at least the following information:

i) The loading conditions upon which the design of this vessel is approved.

ii) The results of the calculations of still water bending moments and shear forces.

iii) Permissible limits of still water bending moments and shear forces and, where applicable, limitations due to torsional and lateral loads.

iv) Maximum allowable local lower decks and double bottom loading.

v) If cargoes other than bulk cargoes are contemplated, such as different deck cargoes, they are to be listed together with any specific instructions for loading.

vi) Maximum allowable load on deck and hatch covers. If the vessel is not approved to carry load on deck or hatch covers, that fact is to be clearly stated in the loading manual.

vii) Information on the heavy ballast draft forward used for the fore-end strengthening required in 3-2-4/15.

conditions</td></tr><tr><td>2.6.10</td><td>short voyages (e.g. half bunker)</td></tr><tr><td>2.6.11</td><td>tank cleaning conditions</td></tr><tr><td>2.6.12</td><td>docking conditions afloat</td></tr></table>

## 7.5 Language

The loading manual is to be prepared in, or is to include, a language understood by the user. English may be considered to be a language understood by the user.

## 9 Loading Instrument (2024)

In addition to the loading manual indicated in [5.1] , Category I vessels of 100 m (328 ft) or more in length are to be provided with a loading instrument verified in accordance with [9] . For Computer Software for Onboard Stability Calculations, additional requirements in Appendix 3-3-A7 are to be applied.

## 9.1 Type

A loading instrument is to be digital. A single point loading instrument is not acceptable.

## 9.3 Functional Requirements and Information (2024)

The requirements of the loading instrument include, but not limited to, the following:

The instrument is to be type approved, where applicable.

The instrument is to be based on the final data of the vessel.

The number and position of read-out points are satisfactory.

The relevant limits for all read-out points are satisfactory.

The verification of the loading instrument is to be in accordance with 3-7-3/7.

## Commentary:

See IACS Recommendation No. 48 for recommendations on the approval of loading instruments.

End of Commentary

## 9.5 Language (2024)

The operation manual and the instrument output are to be prepared in, or are to include, a language understood by the user. If this language is not English, a translation into English is to be included.

## 11 Annual Surveys (2024)

The annual surveys are to be in accordance with 7-3-2/1.1.5.

PART 3

C H A P T E R 2

Hull Structures and Arrangements

A P P E N D I X 3

# Loading Manuals and Loading Instruments: Additional Requirements for Bulk Carriers, Ore Carriers and Combination Carriers 150 Meters (492 Feet) and above in Length ( )

1 Objective (2024)

## 1.1 Goal

The vessels covered in this section are to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goals</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact condition, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 2</td><td>Resist structural failure associated with accidental conditions.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT 3</td><td>Establish procedures, plans and instructions for operations concerning the safety of the personnel, vessel, and protection of the environment. (ISM Code 7)</td></tr></table>

## 1.2 Functional Requirements

To achieve the above stated goals, the design, construction, installation, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>The loading conditions are to be properly defined to cover the critical cases for the intended service with the calculated still water bending moment and shear force to ensure the sufficient hull girder longitudinal strength in intact conditions.</td></tr></table>

3 Loading Manuals and Loading Instruments: Additional Requirements for Bulk Carriers, Ore Carriers and Combination Carriers 150 Meters (492 Feet) and above in

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>The hull girder longitudinal strength in each cargo hold flooded conditions is to be adequate to reduce the risk of structure failure for bulk carriers where there is no double side skin construction with a sufficient width.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>Means is to be provided to enable the Master to quickly perform the calculations to ensure the intended loading conditions meeting the designed limits of hull girder strength and local strength.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Safety Management (MGMT)</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT-FR1</td><td>Information is to be provided to enable the vessel to load and unload cargo safely.</td></tr><tr><td>MGMT-FR2</td><td>Information is to be provided to enable to the vessel to operate within the designed maximum and minimum limits of cargo mass of each cargo hold and adjacent two cargo holds.</td></tr></table>

The functional requirements covered in the cross-referenced Rules are also to be met.

## 1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved. Refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 2 Application (2024)

The requirements in this Appendix apply to bulk carriers, ore carriers and combination carriers having a freeboard length $\left( \begin{array} { l } { L _ { f } } \end{array} \right)$ , as defined in 3-1-1/3.3, of 150 m (492 ft) and above. Unless otherwise stated, these requirements are additional to those in Appendix 3-2-A2.

## Commentary:

This Appendix is based IACS UR S1A “Additional Requirements for Loading Conditions, Loading Manuals and Loading Instruments for Bulk Carriers, Ore Carriers and Combination Carriers”

## End of Commentary

## 3 <No Text>

## 5 Loading Manual

## 5.1 Required Information

## 5.1.1 Permissible Limits

In addition to 3-2-A2/7.1, the loading manual is to include the following information:

5.1.1(a) For bulk carriers specified in [5C-3-A5a/1] where [5C-3-A5a] is applicable, (2024)

i) The permissible limits of still water bending moments and shear forces in the hold flooded condition in accordance with 5C-3-3/3.1 and [5C-3-A5a] .

ii) The still water bending moment limits are to be presented in the form of an envelope curve for all combinations of loading conditions and flooded holds.

5.1.1(b) The cargo hold(s) or combination of cargo holds that might be empty at full draft. If it is not permitted to have an empty cargo hold at full draft, this is to be clearly stated in the loading manual.

## 3 Loading Manuals and Loading Instruments: Additional Requirements for Bulk Carriers, Ore Carriers and Combination Carriers 150 Meters (492 Feet) and above in Length ( )

5.1.1(c) Maximum allowable and minimum required mass ofcontents ofeach cargo hold and double bottom space in way thereof, as a function of the draft at the mid length of the hold.

5.1.1(d) Maximum allowable and minimum required mass of contents of two cargo holds and double bottom spaces forward and aft of any cargo hold bulkhead, as a function of the mean draft. This mean draft may be taken as the average of the drafts at the mid-length of two holds.

## 5.1.2 Loading Rate and Sequence

5.1.2(a) The maximum rate of ballast change

5.1.2(b) An instruction that a loading plan is to be agreed with the terminal on the basis of the achievable rates of change of ballast.

5.1.2(c) Typical sequence of loading from commencement to full deadweight or any contemplated part load conditions. Where applicable, homogeneous conditions and alternate loading conditions are to be included. The typical loading sequences shall be developed with due attention being paid to the loading rate, the deballasting capacity and applicable strength limitations. The Annex to this Appendix and [TABLE 2] contain, as guidance only, an example ofa Loading Sequence Summary Form and aspects that may be considered in developing the sequence.

5.1.2(d) Typical sequences for change of ballast at sea, where applicable.

## 5.3 Loading Conditions

The above information is to be based on the intended service conditions. See [TABLE 1] for the selection of loading conditions, which replaces 3-2-A2/7.3 TABLE 1 for the vessels covered by this Appendix.

## 7 Loading Instrument

## 7.1 Required Verifications

In addition to 3-2-A2/9.3, at least the following aspects are to be demonstrated to the Surveyor for his/her verification:

## 7.1.1

That the instrument can easily and quickly perform calculations to determine that the permissible values at the specified points along the vessel will not be exceeded in any loaded or ballast condition;

## 7.1.2

That the relevant limits for the mass ofcontents ofeach cargo hold and double bottom spaces in way thereof, as a function of the draft at the mid-hold position, are satisfactory;

## 7.1.3

That the relevant limits for the mass of contents of two cargo holds and double bottom spaces forward and aft of any cargo hold bulkhead, as a function of the mean draft in way of these holds, are satisfactory;

## 7.1.4 (2024)

Where applicable for bulk carriers as specified in [5C-3-A5a/1] , that the relevant limits for the still water bending moments and shear forces in any one hold flooded conditions in accordance with 5C-3-3/3.1 and [5C-3-A5a] are satisfactory.

## Notes:

1 Heaviest cargo can be carried and the draft is corresponding to the summer load water line. Loaded holds may not be filled completely with cargo.

2 Lightest cargo can be carried at the summer load water line. Loaded holds may or may not be filled completely with cargo.

3 Heaviest cargo loaded in all cargo holds at the same filling ratio (cargo volume/hold cubic capacity) and at the draft corresponding to the summer load water line. All loaded holds may not be filled up with cargo.

4 Homogeneous loading condition. All cargo holds are filled completely with cargo and the draft is corresponding to the summer load water line.

5 Conditions during loading/unloading are also to be included.

# Hull Structures and Arrangements

A P P E N D I X 4

Buckling Strength of Longitudinal Strength Members for Vessels Over 61 m (200 ft) in Length

## 1 Application (2025)

When compliance with this Appendix is required in the applicable Rules and Guides, these requirements apply to plate panels and longitudinals subject to hull girder bending and shear stresses. This Appendix is not applicable to vessels with the SafeHull SH notation.

## 3 Elastic Buckling Stresses

## 3.1 Elastic Buckling of Plates

## 3.1.1 Compression (2024)

The ideal elastic buckling stress is given by:

$$
\sigma_ {E} = 0. 9 m E \left(\frac {t _ {b}}{s}\right) ^ {2} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , psi)}
$$

For plating with longitudinal stiffeners (parallel to compressive stress) as indicated in [FIGURE 1] :

$$
m = \frac {8 . 4}{\Psi + 1 . 1} \mathrm{for} (0 \leq \Psi \leq 1)
$$

For plating with transverse stiffeners (perpendicular to compressive stress) as indicated in [FIGURE 1] :

$$
m = c \left[ 1 + \left(\frac {s}{\ell}\right) ^ {2} \right] ^ {2} \frac {2 . 1}{\Psi + 1 . 1} \mathrm{for} (0 \leq \Psi \leq 1)
$$

where

$$
E = 2. 0 6 \times 1 0 ^ {5} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2} (2 1, 0 0 0 \mathrm{kgf} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2}, 3 0 \times 1 0 ^ {6} \mathrm{psi})
$$

$t _ { b }$ = net thickness of plating, in mm (in.), after making standard deductions as given in [TABLE 1A] or [TABLE 1B] , as applicable

s = shorter side of plate panel, in mm (in.)

l = longer side of plate panel, in mm (in.)

C 1.3 when plating stiffened by floors or deep girders

= 1.21 when stiffeners are angles or T-sections

= 1.10 when stiffeners are bulb flats

= 1.05 when stiffeners are flat bars

= ratio of smallest to largest compressive stress, $\sigma _ { a }$ (see [7.1] ), varying linearly across panel.

## 3.1.2 Shear

The ideal elastic buckling stress is given by:

$$
\tau_ {E} = 0. 9 k _ {t} E \left(\frac {t _ {b}}{s}\right) ^ {2} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , psi)}
$$

where

$$
k _ {t} = 5. 3 4 + 4 \left(\frac {s}{\ell}\right) ^ {2}
$$

$E , t _ { b } ,$ and are as defined in [3.1.1]

## 3.3 Elastic Buckling of Longitudinals

## 3.3.1 Column Buckling without Rotation of the Cross Section

For the column buckling mode (perpendicular to plane of plating), the ideal elastic buckling stress is given by:

$$
\sigma_ {E} = \frac {E I _ {a}}{c _ {1} A \ell^ {2}} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , psi)}
$$

where

$I _ { a }$ = moment of inertia, in cm<sup>4</sup> (in<sup>4</sup>), of longitudinal, including plate flange and calculated with thickness as specified in [3.1.1]

$A$ = cross-sectional area, in cm<sup>2</sup> (in<sup>2</sup>), of longitudinal, including plate flange and calculated with thickness as specified in [3.1.1]

l = span, in m (ft), of longitudinal

$c _ { 1 }$ = 1000 (1000, 14.4)

$E$ = as defined in [3.1.1]

## 3.3.2 Torsional Buckling Mode

The ideal elastic buckling stress for the torsional mode is given by:

$$
\sigma_ {E} = \frac {\pi^ {2} E I _ {w}}{1 0 c _ {1} I _ {p} \ell^ {2}} \left(m ^ {2} + \frac {K}{m ^ {2}}\right) + 0. 3 8 5 E \frac {I _ {t}}{I _ {p}} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , psi)}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} K & = & c _ {2} \frac {C \ell^ {4}}{\pi^ {4} E I _ {w}} \\ m & = & \text { number   of   half   waves   given   by   [TABLE 2]} \\ E & = & \text { as   defined   in   [3.1.1]} \\ c _ {2} & = & 1 0 ^ {6} (1 0 ^ {6}, 2 0 7 3 6) \\ I _ {t} & = & \text { St.   Venant's   moment   of   inertia,   in   cm } ^ {4} (\text { in } ^ {4}), \text { of   profile   (without   plate   flange) } \\ & = & c _ {3} \frac {h _ {w} t _ {w} ^ {3}}{3} \quad \text { for   flat   bars   (slabs) } \\ & = & c _ {3} \frac {1}{3} \left[ h _ {w} t _ {w} ^ {3} + b _ {f} t _ {f} ^ {3} \left(1 - 0. 6 3 \frac {t _ {f}}{b _ {f}}\right) \right] \text { for   flanged   profiles } \\ c _ {3} & = & 1 0 ^ {- 4} (1 0 ^ {- 4}, 1. 0) \\ I _ {p} & = & \text { polar   moment   of   inertia,   in   cm } ^ {4} (\text { in } ^ {4}), \text { of   profile   about   connection   of   stiffener   to   plate } \\ & = & c _ {3} \frac {h _ {w} ^ {3} t _ {w}}{3} \quad \text { for   flat   bars   (slabs) } \\ & = & c _ {3} \left(\frac {h _ {w} ^ {3} t _ {w}}{3} + h _ {w} ^ {2} b _ {f} t _ {f}\right) \quad \text { for   flanged   profiles } \end{array}
$$

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$I_w$ = warping constant, in cm$^6$ (in$^6$), of profile about connection of stiffener to plate
= $c_4 \frac{h_w^3 t_w^3}{36}$ for flat bars (slabs)
= $c_4 \left( \frac{t_f b_f^3 h_w^2}{12} \right)$ for “Tee” profiles
= $c_4 \frac{b_f^3 h_w^2}{12 (b_f + h_w)^2} \left[ t_f (b_f^2 + 2b_f h_w + 4h_w^2) + 3t_w b_f h_w \right]$ for angles and bulb profiles
$c_4$ = $10^{-6} (10^{-6}, 1.0)$ $h_w$ = web height, in mm (in.)
$t_w$ = web thickness, in mm (in.), after making standard deductions as specified in [3.1.1]
$b_f$ = flange width, in mm (in.)
$t_f$ = flange thickness, in mm (in.), after making standard deductions as specified in [3.1.1] For profiles the mean thickness of the bulb is to be used.
$\ell$ = span of profile, in m (ft)
$s$ = spacing of profiles, in mm (in.)
$C$ = spring stiffness exerted by supporting plate panel
= $\frac{k_p E t_p^3}{3s \left( 1 + \frac{1.33 k_p h_w t_p^3}{s t_w^3} \right)}$ N (kgf, lbf)
$k_p$ = $1 - \eta_p$, not to be taken less than zero
$t_p$ = plate thickness, in mm (in.), after making standard deductions as specified in [3.1.1]
$\eta_p$ = $\frac{\sigma_a}{\sigma_{Ep}}$ $\sigma_\alpha$ = calculated compressive stress. For longitudinals, see [7.1]
$\sigma_{Ep}$ = elastic buckling stress of supporting plate as calculated in [3.1]
</div>

For flanged profiles, $k _ { p }$ need not be taken less than 0.1.

## 3.3.3 Web and Flange Buckling

For web plate of longitudinals the ideal buckling stress is given by:

$$
\sigma_ {E} = 3. 8 E \left(\frac {t _ {w}}{h _ {w}}\right) ^ {2} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2} (\mathrm{kgf} / \mathrm{mm} ^ {2}, \mathrm{psi})
$$

For flanges on angles and T-sections of longitudinals, the following requirements apply:

$$
\frac {b _ {f}}{t _ {f}} \leq 1 5
$$

$b _ { f }$ = flange width, in mm (in.), for angles, half the flange width for T-sections.

$t _ { f }$ = as built flange thickness, in mm (in.)

## 5 Critical Buckling Stresses

## 5.1 Compression

The critical buckling stress in compression, $\sigma _ { c }$ , is determined as follows:

$$
\sigma_ {c} = \sigma_ {E}
$$

when

$$
\sigma_ {E} \leq \frac {\sigma_ {F}}{2}
$$

$$
= \sigma_ {F} \left(1 - \frac {\sigma_ {F}}{4 \sigma_ {E}}\right)
$$

when

$$
\sigma_ {E} > \frac {\sigma_ {F}}{2}
$$

where

$\sigma _ { F }$ = yield stress of material, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, lbf/in<sup>2</sup>). σ is to be taken as 235 N/mm<sup>2</sup> (24 kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, 34,000 psi) for mild steel.

$\sigma _ { E }$ = ideal elastic buckling stress calculated according to [3]

## 5.3 Shear

The critical buckling stress in shear, , is determined as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \tau_ {c} & = & \tau_ {E} \\ & = & \tau_ {F} \left(1 - \frac {\tau_ {F}}{4 \tau_ {E}}\right) \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{l l} \text {when} & \tau_ {E} \leq \frac {\tau_ {F}}{2} \\ \text {when} & \tau_ {E} > \frac {\tau_ {F}}{2} \end{array}
$$

where

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$\tau_{F} = \frac{\sigma_{F}}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sigma_F =$ as given in [5.1]   
$\tau_{E} =$ ideal elastic buckling stress in shear calculated according to [3.1.2]
</div>

## 7 Working Stress

## 7.1 Longitudinal Compressive Stress

The compressive stresses are given in the following formula:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \sigma_ {a} & = c _ {5} \frac {M _ {w} + M _ {s w}}{I _ {n}} y \quad \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , lbf / i n ^ {2})} \\ & = \text { minimum } 3 0 / Q \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (3.1 / Q kgf / m m ^ {2} , 4400 / Q lbf / i n ^ {2})} \end{array}
$$

where

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
$M_{sw} =$ still water bending moment, as given in 3-2-1/3.7.1(a), in kN-m (tf-m, Ltf-ft)
</div>

$M _ { w }$ = wave bending moment, as given in 3-2-1/3.7.1(a), in kN-m (tf-m, Ltf-ft)

$I _ { n }$ = moment of inertia, in cm<sup>4</sup> (in<sup>4</sup>), of the hull girder

$y$ = vertical distance, in m (ft), from the neutral axis to the considered point

Q = as defined in 3-2-1/5.3 (1.0 for ordinary strength steel)

= 10<sup>5</sup> (10<sup>5</sup>, 322,560)

$M _ { w }$ and $M _ { s w }$ are to be taken as sagging or hogging bending moments, respectively, for members above or below the neutral axis.

## 7.3 Shear Stresses

## 7.3.1 Ships without Effective Longitudinal Bulkheads

The working shear stress, $\tau _ { a }$ , in the side shell of ships without effective longitudinal bulkheads is given by the following formula:

$$
\tau_ {a} = c _ {6} \frac {(F _ {s w} + F _ {w}) m _ {s}}{2 t _ {s} I} \mathrm {N / m m ^ {2} (kgf / m m ^ {2} , lbf / i n^ {2})}
$$

where

= moment of inertia of the hull girder section, in $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 4 } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 4 } ) .$ , at the section under consideration.

first moment, in cm<sup>3</sup> (in<sup>3</sup>), about the neutral axis of the area of the effective longitudinal material $m _ { s }$ = between the horizontal level at which the shear stress is being determined and the vertical extremity of effective longitudinal material, taken at the position under consideration.

$t _ { s }$ = thickness of the side shell plating, in cm (in.), at the position under consideration.

$F _ { s w }$ hull girder shearing force in still water, in kN (tf, Ltf). See 3-2-1/3.3.

$F _ { w }$ = $F _ { w p }$ or $F _ { w n }$ , in kN (tf, Ltf), as specified by 3-2-1/3.5.3, depending upon loading

$c _ { 6 }$ = 10 (10, 2240)

## 7.3.2 Ships with Two or More Effective Longitudinal Bulkheads

The working shear stress, , in the side shell or longitudinal bulkhead plating is to be calculated by an acceptable method and in accordance with 3-2-1/3.9.4.

## 9 Scantling Criteria

## 9.1 Buckling Stress (2024)

The design buckling stress, $\sigma _ { c }$ , of plate panels and longitudinals (as calculated in [5.1] ) is to be such that:

$$
\sigma_ {c} \geq \beta \sigma_ {a}
$$

where

$\beta$ = 1 for plating and for web plating of stiffeners (local buckling)

$\beta$ = 1.1 for stiffeners

The critical buckling stress, , of plate panels (as calculated in [5.3] ) is to be such that:

$$
\tau_ {c} \geq \tau_ {a}
$$

where

$\tau _ { a }$ = the working shear stress in the plate panel under consideration, in N/mm<sup>2</sup> (kgf/mm<sup>2</sup>, lbf/in<sup>2</sup>), as determined by [7.3] .

Alternatively for transversely framed vessels between 61 meters (200 feet) and 90 meters (295 feet) in length, the deck and bottom plate may be taken not less than:

$$
t = \frac {s}{4 5} \sqrt {\frac {S M _ {R}}{S M _ {A}}} \cdot \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} + t _ {k} \mathrm{mm(in.)}
$$

where

t = thickness of bottom shell or deck plating, in mm (in.)

$t _ { k }$ = Standard deduction as given in [TABLE 1A] or [TABLE 1B] as applicable, in mm(in.)

S = frame spacing, in mm (in.)

$S M _ { R }$ hull girder section modulus required by 3-2-1/3, at amidships in $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } { - } \mathrm { m } ( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } { - } \mathrm { f t } )$

$S M _ { A }$ = bottom or deck hull girder section modulus at amidships, in cm<sup>2</sup>-m $( \mathrm { i n } ^ { 2 } { - } \mathrm { f t } )$

Q = as defined in 3-2-1/5.3

Hull Structures and Arrangements

A P P E N D I X 5

Guidelines for Calculating Bending Moment and Shear Force in Rudders and Rudder Stocks

## 1 Application (2024)

Bending moments, shear forces and reaction forces of rudders, stocks and bearings may be calculated according to this Appendix for the types of rudders indicated. Moments and forces on rudders of different types or shapes than those shown are to be calculated using alternative methods and will be considered based on submitted documents and calculations supporting the review.

Commentary:

The requirements of Appendix 3-2-A5 are based on IACS UR S10 Annex.

End of Commentary

## 3 Spade Rudders

## 3.1 Rudder Blade

## 3.1.1 Shear Force (2020)

For regular spade rudders as shown in [FIGURE 1] (a), the shear force, , at a horizontal section of the rudder above baseline is given by the following equation:

$$
V (z) = \frac {z C _ {R}}{A} \left[ c _ {\ell} + \frac {z}{2 \ell_ {R}} \left(c _ {u} - c _ {\ell}\right) \right] \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

where

z = distance from the rudder baseline to the horizontal section under consideration, in m (ft)

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force, as defined in 3-2-14/3, in kN (tf, Ltf )

$A$ total projected area of rudder blade in m $^ \colon ( \mathrm { f t } ^ { 2 } )$ , as defined in 3-2-14/3

$c _ { \ell } , c _ { u }$ and $\ell _ { R }$ are dimensions as indicated in [FIGURE 1] (a), in m (ft).

For spade rudders with embedded rudder trunks let deep in the rudder blade, as shown in [FIGURE 1] (b), the shear forces at rudder horizontal sections above rudder baseline in areas $A _ { 1 } ,$ and $A _ { 2 } ,$ are given by the following equations:

$$
V \left(z ^ {\prime}\right) _ {1} = \frac {z ^ {\prime} C _ {R 1}}{A _ {1}} \left[ c _ {u} - \frac {z ^ {\prime}}{2 \ell_ {\ell}} \left(c _ {u} - c _ {b}\right) \right] \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf),overarea} A _ {1}
$$

$$
V (z) _ {2} = \frac {z C _ {R 2}}{A _ {2}} \left[ c _ {\ell} + \frac {z}{2 \ell_ {b}} (c _ {b} - c _ {\ell}) \right] \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf),overarea} A _ {2}
$$

where

$$
{ z I } { = } { \ell _ { \mathrm{~R~} } - \mathrm{~Z~} }
$$

C<sub>R1</sub> = rudder force over rudder area $A _ { I } ,$ in kN (tf, Ltf)

$$
= \frac {A _ {1}}{A} C _ {R}
$$

C<sub>R2</sub> = rudder force over rudder area $A _ { 2 } ,$ in kN (tf, Ltf)

$A _ { I }$ = partial rudder blade area above neck bearing and below rudder top, in mm<sup>2</sup> (ft<sup>2</sup>)

$A _ { 2 }$ = partial rudder blade area above rudder baseline and below neck bearing, in mm<sup>2</sup> (ft<sup>2</sup>)

and $C _ { R }$ are as indicated in [3.1.1] .

$c _ { \ell } , c _ { b } , c _ { u } , \ell _ { u }$ and $\ell _ { b }$ are dimensions as illustrated in [FIGURE 1] (b).

## 3.1.2 Bending Moment (1 July 2024)

For regular spade rudders, bending moment, $M ( z )$ , at a horizontal section z meters (feet) above the baseline of the rudder is given by the following equation:

$$
M (z) = \frac {z ^ {2} C _ {R}}{2 A} \left[ c _ {\ell} + \frac {z}{3 \ell_ {R}} \left(c _ {u} - c _ {\ell}\right) \right] \mathrm{kN-m,(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

The moment at the top of the cone coupling is applicable for the connection between the rudder and rudder stock.

For spade rudders with embedded rudder trunk, the bending moment at a horizontal section within area $A _ { 1 }$ is obtained from the following:

$$
M (z ^ {\prime}) _ {1} = \frac {(z ^ {\prime}) ^ {2} C _ {R 1}}{2 A _ {1}} \left[ c _ {u} - \frac {z ^ {\prime}}{3 \ell_ {\ell}} (c _ {u} - c _ {b}) \right] \mathrm{kN-m,(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

With the maximum bending moment $M _ { 1 }$ over area equals to:

$$
M _ {1} = C _ {R 1} \ell_ {\ell} \left[ 1 - \frac {2 c _ {b} + c _ {u}}{3 (c _ {b} + c _ {u})} \right] \mathrm{kN-m,(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

For spade rudders with embedded rudder trunk, the bending moment at a horizontal section within area $A _ { 2 }$ is obtained from the following:

$$
M (z) _ {2} = \frac {z ^ {2} C _ {R 2}}{2 A _ {2}} \left[ c _ {\ell} + \frac {z}{3 \ell_ {b}} \left(c _ {b} - c _ {\ell}\right) \right] \mathrm{kN-m}, (\mathrm{tf-m,Ltf-ft})
$$

With the maximum bending moment $M _ { 2 }$ over area $A _ { 2 }$ equals to:

$$
M _ {2} = C _ {R 2} \ell_ {b} \frac {2 c _ {\ell} + c _ {b}}{3 (c _ {\ell} + c _ {b})} \mathrm{kN-m,(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

where $z , z ^ { \prime } , C _ { R 1 } , C _ { R 2 } , A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , c _ { \ell } , c _ { u }$ and $\ell _ { R }$ are as defined in [3.1.1] .

## 3.1.3 Load Cases for Spade Rudders with Embedded Rudder Trunk (1 July 2024)

For spade rudders with embedded rudder trunk, the strength is to be checked against the shear forces and bending moments as defined in 3-2-A5/3.1.1 and 3-2-A5/3.1.2 for the following two cases:

i) Pressure applied on the entire rudder area

ii) Pressure applied only on rudder area below the middle of neck bearing

## 3.3 Lower Stock

## 3.3.1 Shear Force

For regular spade rudder, the shear force, , at any section of the lower stock between the top of the rudder and the neck bearing is given by the following equation:

$$
V _ {\ell} = C _ {R} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

For spade rudder with embedded rudder trunk, the shear force at any section of the stock between the top of the rudder and the neck bearing is given by the following equation:

$$
V _ {\ell} = \frac {M _ {2} - M _ {1}}{\ell_ {u} + \ell_ {\ell}} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

where $C _ { R } , \ell _ { \ell } ,$ and $\ell _ { u }$ are as defined in [3.1.1] .

## 3.3.2 Bending Moment at Neck Bearing

For regular spade rudder, the bending moment in the rudder stock at the neck bearing, $M _ { n }$ , is given by the following equation:

$$
M _ {n} = C _ {R} \left[ \ell_ {\ell} + \frac {\ell_ {R} (2 c _ {\ell} + c _ {u})}{3 (c _ {\ell} + c _ {u})} \right] \mathrm{kN-m(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

where

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force as defined in 3-2-14/3

$c _ { \ell } , c _ { u } , \ell _ { \ell }$ and $\ell _ { R }$ are dimensions as indicated in [FIGURE 1] , in m (ft.).

For spade rudder with embedded rudder trunk, the bending moment in the rudder stock at the neck bearing is given by the following equation:

$$
M _ {n} = M _ {2} - M _ {1} \mathrm{kN} - \mathrm{m(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

where $M _ { 1 }$ and $M _ { 2 }$ as defined in [3.1.2] .

Where partial submergence of the rudder leads to a higher bending moment in the rudder stock at the neck bearing (compared with the fully submerged condition), $M _ { n }$ is to be calculated based on the most severe partially submerged condition.

## 3.5 Moment at Top of Upper Stock Taper

For regular spade rudder, the bending moment in the upper rudder stock at the top of the taper, $M _ { t }$ , is given by the following equation:

$$
M _ {t} = C _ {R} \left[ \ell_ {\ell} + \frac {\ell_ {R} (2 c _ {\ell} + c _ {u})}{3 (c _ {\ell} + c _ {u})} \right] \times \left[ \frac {(\ell_ {u} + \ell_ {R} + \ell_ {\ell} - z _ {t})}{\ell_ {u}} \right] \mathrm{kN-m,(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

For spade rudder with embedded rudder trunk, the bending moment in the upper rudder stock at the top of the taper is given by the following equation:

$$
M _ {t} = M _ {R} \left[ \frac {(\ell_ {R} + \ell_ {u} - z _ {t})}{\ell_ {u}} \right] \mathrm{kN-m(tf-m,Ltf-ft)}
$$

where

$z _ { t }$ = distance from the rudder baseline to the top of the upper rudder stock taper in m (ft.)

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force, as defined in [3.1.1]

$M _ { R }$ = is the greater of $M _ { 1 }$ and $M _ { 2 } ,$ as defined in [3.1.2]

$c _ { \ell } , c _ { u } , \ell _ { \ell } , \ell _ { u }$ and $\ell _ { R }$ are dimensions as indicated in [FIGURE 1] , in m (ft).

## 3.7 Bearing Reaction Forces

For regular spade rudder, the reaction forces at the bearings are given by the following equations:

$P _ { u }$ = reaction force at the upper bearing

$$
= - \frac {M _ {n}}{\ell_ {u}} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

$P _ { n }$ = reaction force at the neck bearing

$$
= C _ {R} + \frac {M _ {n}}{\ell_ {u}} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}
$$

For spade rudder with embedded rudder trunk, the reaction forces at the bearings are given by the following equations:

$$
{P _ {u}} = {- \frac {M _ {n}}{\ell_ {u} + \ell_ {\ell}} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}}
$$

$$
{P _ {n}} = {C _ {R} + P _ {u} \mathrm{kN(tf,Ltf)}}
$$

where

$M _ { n }$ = bending moment at the neck bearing, as defined in [3.3.2]

$C _ { R }$ = rudder force, as defined in 3-2-14/3.

is as indicated in [FIGURE 1] , in m (ft).

# Hull Structures and Arrangements

A P P E N D I X 7

# Review of Portable Industrial Equipment and Modules

## 1 Objective (2024)

## 1.1 Goals

Industrial equipment and modules defined in [2.1] .1 is to be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to:

<table><tr><td>Goal No.</td><td>Goals</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 1</td><td>In the intact conditions, have sufficient structural strength to withstand the environmental conditions, loading conditions, and operational loads anticipated during the design life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU 3</td><td>Provide protection to persons onboard, the environment and required safety services.</td></tr><tr><td>SAFE 1.1</td><td>Minimize danger to persons on board, the vessel, and surrounding equipment/installations from hazards associated with machinery and systems.</td></tr><tr><td>CARGO SG7</td><td>Have measures to mitigate risk to vessel&#x27;s stability due to cargo shifting or cargo liquefaction.</td></tr><tr><td>FIR 1</td><td>Prevent the occurrence of fire and explosion (SOLAS II-2/Reg 2.1.1).</td></tr><tr><td>EER 1</td><td>Provide means of escape so that persons on board can safely and swiftly escape to a protected place of refuge, muster station, or embarkment station (SOLAS II-2/Reg 13.1).</td></tr></table>

## 1.2 Functional Requirements

In order to achieve the above-stated goals, the design, construction, and maintenance are to be in accordance with the following functional requirements:

<table><tr><td>Functional Requirement No.</td><td>Functional Requirements</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Structure (STRU)</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR1</td><td>Deck foundations in way of industrial equipment and industrial modules are to be designed to withstand the design loads for operations during the anticipated installation.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR2</td><td>Scantlings are to have sufficient strength to protect personnel when subjected to the loads anticipated throughout the service life.</td></tr><tr><td>STRU-FR3</td><td>Scantlings are to be maintained so that structure will continue to satisfy all Goals and Functional Requirements.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Safety (SAFE)</td></tr><tr><td>SAFE-FR1</td><td>Accurate documentation detailing the installation of industrial equipment and modules is to be provided.</td></tr><tr><td>SAFE-FR2</td><td>Hazardous areas should be restricted to minimize the potential risks that might affect the safety of the ship, persons on board and equipment.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Cargo (CARGO)</td></tr><tr><td>CARGO-FR1</td><td>Securing devices used for industrial equipment and industrial modules are to be of sufficient quantity and quality and so designed to withstand the design loads for operations during the anticipated installation.</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Fire Safety (FIR)</td></tr><tr><td>FIR-FR1</td><td>Means are to be provided to minimize the spread of flammable, explosive, or toxic gas to non-hazardous areas.</td></tr><tr><td>FIR-FR2</td><td>Extinguishing and detection measures appropriate to the hazards concerned are to be provided.</td></tr><tr><td>FIR-FR3</td><td>Hazards to life from smoke and toxic products generated during a fire in spaces where persons normally work or live are to be provided. (SOLAS II-2)</td></tr><tr><td>FIR-FR4</td><td>The fire growth potential in every space of the ship is to be limited. (SOLAS II-2)</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2">Escape, Evacuation, Rescue (EER)</td></tr><tr><td>EER-FR1</td><td>Hatches, doors, and windows are to be arranged so that means of escape, evacuation and access are not restricted. (SOLAS II-2)</td></tr></table>

The functional requirements in the cross-referenced Rules are to be met.

## 1.3 Compliance

A vessel is considered to comply with the goals and functional requirements within the scope of classification when the applicable prescriptive requirements are complied with or when an alternative arrangement has been approved. Refer to Part 1D, Chapter 2.

## 2 General (2025)

Where industrial equipment, systems, tanks and/or other industrial items (industrial equipment) are installed aboard a vessel without a Classification Notation for specialized functional service, the impact on the vessel safety is to be reviewed in accordance with this appendix.

Industrial modules may be used for various purposes, such as Workshops, Instrument Control, MCC/ Battery/Switchgear Rooms, Laboratories, Wireline Units, ROV Control Room, etc. They may not be used for accommodations or living spaces and they are to be unmanned during heavy weather and sufficient space for the entire complement of personal assigned to work in the module(s) is provided in a deckhouse, superstructure, or module complying fully with applicable structural requirements

Commentary:

Refer to the ABS Requirements for Portable Accommodation Modules for requirements for modules used for accommodation, living spaces, or modules manned during heavy weather.

## End of Commentary

The Installation of industrial modules and equipment is subject to survey in presence of and to the satisfaction of the attending Surveyor in accordance with Appendix 7-A1-17 of the ABS Rules for Survey After Construction (Part 7), as applicable. Flag Administration requirements are to be considered in addition to this Appendix.

## 2.1 Applicability and Types of Industrial Modules (2024)

Requirements of this Appendix apply to portable industrial equipment modules where the forces on the cargo deck exceed the rated deck capacity, to any portable industrial equipment module which is not a standard container box or to a securing arrangement which is not covered in the vessel's approved Cargo Securing Manual. Nothing in this Appendix is intended to permit installations of industrial equipment which would require a Classification Notation for specialized functional service.

## 2.3 Background (2024)

The installation of portable industrial equipment, industrial spaces, and workshops has become increasingly prevalent in recent years. Irrespective of the amount of time that portable modules are installed onboard, the potential risks to personnel within and around these modules is of concern and therefore it is imperative that details be reviewed in accordance with this Appendix.

## 3 Submission of Data (2024)

For the installation of industrial equipment and modules, the list of plans in 5D-2-1/7 applies. When a vessel is carrying independent tanks on deck which contain Hazardous and Noxious Liquid Substances, as defined in Section 5D-2-3 of the Rules, International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code), IMO Resolution A.673 (16) and IEC 60092-502, then the list of plans in 5D-2-3/7 applies.

## Commentary:

Flag Administrations may have specific requirements on certification and construction standards of industrial modules tha are manned. When these requirements are applicable and ABS issues statutory certificates, all required documentation should be submitted to ABS.

## End of Commentary

Where a container box is considered an industrial module in accordance with the applicable Rules for the intended purpose, the container is to be confirmed as being certified to a recognized standard and documentation is to be submitted to ABS.

## 5 Structural Review

## 5.1 Arrangements (2024)

A revised General Arrangement drawing is to be submitted for the vessel whenever industrial equipment or modules are installed on deck. This submittal will be kept available for reference by ABS for the duration of the installation. The General Arrangement is to show the exact location of each piece of industrial equipment or modules and is to be furnished to ABS at the start of the project. If the location of equipment changes, then a new arrangement is to be submitted to ABS. At the completion of a project or when all industrial equipment and modules have been removed, a notice shall be furnished to ABS. At this time a clean General Arrangement is not required, provided that it has not changed from the revision which previously reviewed by ABS prior to the installation of the equipment.

Stacked arrangements of industrial modules or equipment require design review by ABS, and are to be surveyed accordingly.

Where isolated deck cargo exceeds the rated deck capacity, the vessel scantlings are to comply with Section 5D-1-4. The vessel structure will be analyzed using standard accelerations applied from the vessel's approved cargo securing manual or the IMO Code ofSafe Practicefor Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code). The resulting stresses in deck members from cargo loadings are not to exceed those values found in 5D-2-2/1.3.

If a vendor provides drawings or documents of design loads or forces, then these design loads are to include appropriate accelerations or dynamic factors for transverse, longitudinal, and vertical loadings as appropriate for the intended service.

## 5.3 Securing Arrangement and Securing Details

Where securing devices used are outside the scope of the vessel’s Cargo Securing Manual, the equipment exceeds rated deck capacity, or a Cargo Securing Manual has not been approved for the vessel, details of securing devices are to be reviewed by ABS. These details may be provided either on a separate drawing or on the General Arrangement. All securing details are to be shown. If the equipment does not exceed the deck capacity and the securing devices are included in the approved Cargo Securing Manual, then the securing is at the discretion of the vessel's crew in accordance with the vessel's Cargo Securing Manual.

## 5.3.1 Welded Fittings (2024)

A welded fitting is a plate clip, bracket or metal stopper which is intended to secure equipment to the vessel. Simple welded fittings may be used to provide securing against sliding. If a welded fitting is intended to resist uplift from over-turning moments, then the horizontal edge is welded to the deck and likewise the vertical edge is welded to the piece of equipment or skid, see [FIGURE 1] .

In some cases, a vendor may request these welded fittings not be welded to their equipment, as shown in [FIGURE 2] . In this case, the fitting may be slotted into a corner casting or fit tightly around an accessible edge. In this case effectiveness of the clips is to be reduced and the weld at the deck sized appropriately.

If welded fittings are the only means of securing, then they are to be provided in both the transverse and longitudinal directions so that they are not loaded at right angles to the weld direction by significant bending forces. These fittings, in their quantity, size, and welds, are to be able to resist the forces of sliding and tipping, with applicable accelerations. Calculations are to be performed to confirm this for both shear and weld strength.

Additional calculations may be necessary to check the bending strength adequacy of the fitting based on the fitting design and the proposed arrangement.

Required details for welded fittings are:

● Plate thickness

Weld size and details

● Dimensions of the clip

● Plate material

## 5.3.2 Lashings including Chain and Wire Rope (2024)

All chains, wire ropes, turnbuckles and all other pieces of lashing equipment being used are to comply with those approved in the vessel’s Cargo Securing Manual, if one is provided. Securing devices not in the Cargo Securing Manual may be used if details of them are provided.

When lashings are used, they are to be able to resist the forces of sliding and tipping, in accordance with the CSS Code.

## Commentary:

The effective direction of a lashing is defined in the IMO Code ofSafe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code) ANNEX 13 which provides reductions in working loads of devices based on the angles formed between the deck and cargo.

## End of Commentary

Required details for lashings are:

● Securing point on deck

● Securing point on the equipment

● Angle of the lash with respect to the deck and respect to the centerline of the vesse

Material and type of lashing (i.e., Chain, wire rope, turnbuckle, shackles, etc.)

Safe Working Load of lashings

## 5.3.3 ISO Fittings

ISO fitting means, any deck socket, twist lock, deck casting, or securing device which is ISO or type approved.

Where ISO fittings are used, cut sheets or manufacturer specifications of all parts are to be provided to ABS; or at a minimum the manufacturer and model are to be noted on the arrangement, securing drawing or furnished to ABS.

## 5.5 Weights (2024)

A static weight is to be provided to ABS for every piece of industrial equipment and modules which exceeds the rated deck capacity. This weight should be noted on the drawing or provided in a separate document.

## Commentary:

The weights are subject to motion based accelerations per the IMO Code ofSafe Practicefor Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code). The CSS Code provides not only vertical accelerations but also transverse and longitudinal sliding and tipping forces.

## End of Commentary

If the vendor or manufacturer of the equipment provides design loads, these loads are to incorporate accelerations consistent with the CSS Code.

## 5.7 Deck Contact Area, Skids and Mounting Frames (2024)

For all industrial equipment and modules, the contact area to the deck foundation is to be specified.

For equipment and modules which sits on a skid or frame, details of the skid are to be provided, including identification of members and how the skid is secured to the deck as well as how the piece of equipment is secured to the skid or frame. When skids, equipment foundations and mounting frames are installed between the vessel cargo deck and industrial module or industrial equipment, they are to be considered as part of the furnished installation.

If the piece of equipment or of the modules have integral contact points which are part of the design, then these contact areas are to be noted on the arrangement drawing. Additionally, vendor drawings, documents and details pertaining to the installation of industrial equipment and modules are to be furnished to ABS.

## 5.9 Equipment Installed Over the Side Shell (2024)

Dynamic loads are to be provided for any piece of equipment which will be used for service over the side of the vessel as a cable reel, ROV frame, A-Frame, davit, or crane.

If the manufacture of such equipment provided design loads then this information is to be furnished to ABS. If dynamic loads exceed the loading from accelerations applied to the static weight per the IMO Code of Safe Practicefor Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code) then these forces may be used. If dynamic forces are included in the design loads it is at the discretion of ABS to determine whether the dynamic forces are sufficient per applicable rules and regulations.

## 7 Statutory

## 7.1 Ventilation (2024)

Ventilation openings and their proximity to hazards and hazardous or noxious cargoes are to comply with the Section 5D-2-3 of the Rules as well as the applicable regulations, including the International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code) and IMO Resolution A.673 (16) and IEC 60092-502. When a piece of equipment or independent tank is installed on deck and modification is necessary to meet the applicable requirements, then a revised ventilation arrangement is to be submitted to ABS for review.

## 7.3 Doors, Windows and Hatches (2024)

Doors, windows, hatches and other tonnage openings are to comply with the Section 5D-2-3 of the Rules as well and applicable regulations, to include their proximity to hazards or cargoes as defined in the rules and the International Codefor the Construction and Equipment ofShips Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code), IMO Resolution A.673 (16) and IEC 60092-502. When a module, a piece of equipment, or independent tank is installed on deck and modification is necessary to meet the applicable requirements, then the appropriate revised plans arrangement is to be submitted to ABS for review.

Hatches which are not used for escape, secondary means or emergency escape and not used for access during normal operations and are located in a hazardous zone, or cargo area are to be welded shut as a suitable means of securing them from access during the time the industrial equipment or independent tanks are installed. The Fire Control Plan is to be revised accordingly.

## 7.5 Fire Control Plans and Lifesaving (2024)

When industrial equipment or modules are installed onboard and the equipment or module is fitted with a fire detection system or additional fire-fighting equipment, details of the system are to be included on the Fire Control Plan and submitted to ABS for review. Additionally, any modification to the vessel's Fire Control Plan as a result of the installation of industrial equipment or modules is to be submitted to ABS for review.

## Commentary:

Where ABS issues statutory certificates on behalf of a flag Administration any modification to the vessel’s life saving arrangement as a result of installation of industrial equipment or modules on a vessel which obstruct, interfere with, or contain products or hazards which either obstruct or interfere with operation of life saving equipment, the vessel’s life saving plan is to be revised in accordance with SOLAS and flag applicable regulations. Surveyor is to endorse the onboard life-saving plan to indicate ABS verification.

## End of Commentary

## 9 Electrical

## 9.1 General (2024)

If industrial equipment or modules are going to be tied into the vessel's electrical systems, then drawings showing the proposed modifications are to provided (i.e., Vessel One Line Diagram, etc.). The electrical systems are to be designed in accordance with the requirements set forth in Part 4, Chapter 8 and Part 5D, as appropriate.

## 9.1.1 Hazardous Zone Plan (2024)

When equipment or tanks are installed on deck and they contain products as defined in the International Code for the Construction and Equipment ofShips Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code), IMO Resolution A.673 (16) and IEC 60092-502, or any other product which generates hazardous for electrical installations, then a hazardous zone plan is to be submitted to ABS for review. The plan should include these areas as defined in the applicable regulations along with an electrical equipment register. See [4-8-4/1.5] and [4-8-4/27] .

## 11 Mechanical, Safety Systems, and Piping (2024)

## 11.1 General (2024)

If industrial equipment and modules are to connect to the vessel's piping systems, mechanical systems or any other host vessel system or service, drawings showing the proposed modifications are to be provided.

Any fixed deck piping system installed for use by portable industrial equipment is to be submitted to ABS for review.

The machinery systems are to be designed in accordance with the requirements set forth in Part 4 and Part 5D, as appropriate. See Part 4, Chapter 6 for piping systems, and Part 4, Chapter 8 for fire safety systems.

## 13 Equipment Designed for Specialized Work (2024)

Where a classification notation for specialized vessel is requested or is mandatory if represents the primary intended service in accordance with 5D-1-1/5 the installation of equipment used for specialized work such as Oil Spill Recovery, Well Intervention or Stimulation, Fire Fighting, Safety Standby, Pipe Laying, Cable Laying, etc. are to comply with the specific section of Part 5D.

## 15 Stability and Tonnage (2024)

For installations of industrial equipment and modules which fall outside the scope of the vessel’s existing stability guidance, documents are to be submitted to ABS for review to the criteria applicable to the vessel. Refer to Section 3-3-1.

For lightship characteristics if vessels undergoing installation of industrial equipment or modules or undergoing modifications see 3-3-1/7.11.

An addendum to the existing approved trim and stability booklet may be required to provide the master with revised operating guidance based on the installed equipment/modules.

## Commentary:

When additional industrial modules of equipment are installed and ABS issues tonnage certificates on behalf of a flag Administration, the additional volume is to be evaluated against the assigned tonnage and flag Administration requirements to determine if an updated tonnage certificate is required to be issued.

## End of Commentary

A P P E N D I X 8

# Buckling Strength Assessment of Ship Structural Elements

## 1 Application and Definitions

## Abbreviations

EPP Elementary Plate Panel, as defined in 3-2-A8/1.2.3(a).

PSM Primary Supporting Member.

SP Stiffened Panel, as defined in 3-2-A8/1.2.3(c).

UP Unstiffened Panel, as defined in 3-2-A8/1.2.3(c).

## 1.1 Application

## Commentary:

The requirements in 3-2-A8 are based on IACS Unified Requirements (UR) S35.

Compliance with the requirements in 3-2-A8/2 is exclusively limited to stiffeners in hatch cover structures.

Compliance with the requirements in 3-2-A8/3 will not become effective until IACS UR S11, UR S11A or other IACS URs are updated to require compliance with UR S35.

## End of Commentary

## 1.1.1 General

## 1.1.1(a) Relevant rule sections

The requirement in Appendix 3-2-A8 establishes a general buckling assessment procedure and is to be applied in conjunction with the sections of the Marine Vessel Rules where Appendix 3-2-A8 is indicated and referred to as Relevant Sections hereafter, as illustrated in 3-2-A8/Figure 1.

FIGURE 1 Overview of Applying 3-2-A8 in Conjunction with Relevant Sections  
![](ABS-Rules_for_Building_and_Classing_Marine_Vessels%E2%80%94Part3-Hull_Construction_and_Equipment/part-0401-0600/images/b45f7b17dc12ec6481c83186d1625ba1d2292fa16d14313847b8e706eb397655.jpg)  
Note: BUF stands for Buckling Utilization Factor, HC stands for Hatch Cover, and HG stands for Hull Girder.

## 1.1.2 Application

1.1.2(a) Sections

The buckling checks are to be performed according to:

3-2-A8/1 for general definitions regarding buckling capacity, allowable buckling utilization factors and buckling check criteria.

● 3-2-A8/2 for the slenderness requirements of longitudinal and transverse stiffeners.

3-2-A8/3 for the prescriptive buckling requirements of plates, longitudinal and transverse stiffeners, primary supporting members and other structures subject to hull girder stresses.

● 3-2-A8/4 for direct strength analysis (usually by finite element method) buckling requirements of hatch cover structural members including plates, stiffeners and primary supporting members.

3-2-A8/5 for the determination of buckling capacities of plate panels, stiffeners, primary supporting members and column structures.

## 1.1.2(b) Buckling assessment

For the buckling assessment of a ship hull girder, a hatch cover or some structural component, the slenderness requirements as defined in 3-2-A8/2 and the buckling requirements as defined in 3-2- A8/3 or 3-2-A8/4 are to be checked as per the requirements of Relevant Sections.

## 1.1.2(c) Alternative methods

This requirement contains the general methods for the determination of buckling capacities of plate panels, stiffeners, primary supporting members, and columns. For special cases not covered in this requirement, such as a whole plate structure with stiffeners in two directions (i.e., a stiffened panel with both primary and secondary stiffeners), other more advanced methods, such as finite element analysis methods, can be used as deemed appropriate by ABS.

## 1.2 Terminology and Assumptions

## 1.2.1 Buckling

1.2.1(a) Buckling strength

Buckling strength or capacity refers to the strength of a structure under in-plane compressions and/ or shear and lateral load. Buckling strength with consideration of the buckling behavior in 3-2- A8/1.2.1(b) gives a lower bound estimate of ultimate capacity, or the maximum load a structural member can carry without suffering major permanent set. For each structural member, its buckling strength is to be taken as corresponding to the most unfavorable or critical buckling mode.

## 1.2.1(b) Buckling behavior

Buckling strength assessment takes into account both elastic buckling and post-buckling behaviors. Post-buckling can consider the internal redistribution of loads depending on the load situation, slenderness and type of structure. Such as for the buckling assessment of plates, generally its positive elastic post-buckling effect can be utilized.

As such, for slender structures, the calculated buckling strength is typically higher than the ideal elastic buckling stress (minimum eigenvalue). Accepting elastic buckling of slender plate panels implies that large elastic deflections and reduced in-plane stiffness may occur at higher buckling utilization levels.

## 1.2.2 Net Scantling Approach

## 1.2.2(a) General

Unless otherwise specified, all the scantling requirements, including slenderness requirements, in this requirement are based on net scantlings obtained by removing full corrosion addition from the gross offered thicknesses.

## 1.2.2(b) Corrosion addition

Corrosion addition referred to in this requirement is defined in Relevant Sections.

## 1.2.2(c) Stress calculation models

The structural models used for the calculation of stresses to be applied for buckling assessment, which are usually based on net scantlings, are defined in Relevant Sections.

## 1.2.3 Structural Idealization

## 1.2.3(a) Elementary plate panel

An elementary plate panel (EPP) is the unstiffened part of the plating between stiffeners and/or primary supporting members. The plate panel length, a, and breadth, b, of the EPP are defined respectively as the longest and shortest plate edges, as shown in 3-2-A8/Figure 2.

## 1.2.3(b) Standard types ofstiffeners

Definitions of the cross-sectional dimensions of typical stiffener types are shown in 3-2-A8/Figure 3, which are flat bars, bulb flats, angles, L2 and T bars. If applicable, other types of stiffeners can be idealized to one of the typical types in 3-2-A8/Figure 3 for buckling check. For the U-type stiffener which is usually fitted in some hatch covers, the definition of its cross-sectional dimensions is shown in 3-2-A8/Figure 4.

Unless otherwise specified, the full span or full length l, in mm, of a stiffener is to be used for buckling check, which equals to the spacing between primary supporting members.

Symbolic dimensions of the cross-sections are as below:

$e _ { f }$ = Distance from attached plating to centre of flange, in mm, as shown in 3-2-A8/ Figure 3. For its detailed definition, refer to 3-2-A8/5, Symbols.

$h _ { w }$ = Depth of stiffener web, in mm, as shown in 3-2-A8/Figure 3 and 3-2-A8/Figure 4.

$t _ { f }$ = Net flange thickness, in mm.

$t _ { p }$ = Net thickness of plate, in mm.

$t _ { w }$ = Net web thickness, in mm.

## 1.2.3(c) Stiffened panel (SP) and Unstiffened panel (UP)

For a panel with relatively strong interactive effect between the stiffener and its attached plate, each stiffener with its attached plate as a whole is to be modelled as a stiffened panel (SP), so as to be able to consider both of its local and global buckling modes.

However, for an EPP, ifits buckling strength can be checked without considering its interactive effect with stiffeners fitted along its edges, it’s to be modelled as an unstiffened panel (UP).

## 1.2.4 Sign Convention

1.2.4(a) Stresses

In this requirement, compressive and shear stresses are to be taken as positive, tension stresses are to be taken as negative.

## 1.3 Assessment Methods and Acceptance Criteria

## 1.3.1 Assessment Methods

1.3.1(a) Method A and Method B

The buckling assessment is to be carried out according to one of the following two methods taking into account different boundary condition types:

Method A: All the edges of the EPP are forced to remain straight (but free to move in the inplane directions) due to the surrounding structure/neighboring plates.

Method B: The edges of the EPP are not forced to remain straight due to low in-plane stiffness at the edges and/or no surrounding structure/neighboring plates.

## 1.3.1(b) SP-A, SP-B, UP-A and UP-B models

For the buckling assessment ofthe stiffened panel (SP) and unstiffened panel (UP) structural models defined in 3-2-A8/1.2.3(c), with application of either Method A or Method B for the plate buckling assessment, the following four buckling assessment models are established:

SP-A: a stiffened panel with application of Method A.

SP-B: a stiffened panel with application of Method B.

UP-A: an unstiffened panel with application of Method A.

UP-B: an unstiffened panel with application of Method B.

## 1.3.2 Buckling Utilization Factor

1.3.2(a)

The utilization factor, , is defined as the ratio between the applied loads and the corresponding buckling capacity.

1.3.2(b)

For combined loads, the utilization factor, , is defined as the ratio of the applied equivalent stress and the corresponding buckling capacity, as shown in 3-2-A8/Figure 5, and is to be taken as:

$$
\eta_ {a c t} = \frac {W _ {a c t}}{W _ {U}} = \frac {1}{\gamma_ {c}}
$$

where

$W _ { a c t }$ = Equivalent applied stress. The actual applied stresses are given in 3-2-A8/3 and 3-2- A8/4 respectively for buckling assessment by prescriptive and direct strength analysis.

$W _ { U }$ = Equivalent buckling capacity. For plates and stiffeners, their respective buckling or ultimate capacities are given in 3-2-A8/5.

$\gamma _ { c }$ = Stress multiplier factor at failure.

For each typical failure mode, the corresponding buckling capacity of the panel is calculated by applying the actual stress combination and then increasing or decreasing the stresses proportionally until collapse occurs (i.e., when the increased or decreased stresses are on a buckling strength interaction curve or surface).

3-2-A8/Figure 5 illustrates the buckling capacity and the buckling utilization factor of a structural member subject to $\sigma _ { x }$ and $\sigma _ { y }$ stresses.

Illustration of Buckling Capacity and Buckling Utilization Factor

## 1.3.3 Allowable Buckling Utilization Factor

1.3.3(a)

The allowable buckling utilization factor is to be taken according to Relevant Sections.

## 1.3.4 Buckling Acceptance Criteria

1.3.4(a)

A structural member is considered to have an acceptable buckling strength if it satisfies the following criterion:

$\eta _ { a c t } \leq \eta _ { a l l }$

where:

= Buckling utilization factor based on the applied stress, defined in 3-2-A8/1.3.2(b).

= Allowable buckling utilization factor as defined in 3-2-A8/1.3.3(a).

$$

b) Flange:

$$

If requirement b) is not fulfilled, the effective free flange outstand, in mm, used in strength assessment including the calculation of actual net section modulus, is to be taken as:

$$
b _ {f - o u t - m a x} = C _ {f} t _ {f} \sqrt {\frac {2 3 5}{R _ {e H}}}
$$

## 3.1.1 Introduction

## 3.1.1(b)

The ship longitudinal extent where the buckling check is performed for structural elements subject to hull girder stresses is to be in accordance with Relevant Sections.

3.1.1(c)

Design load sets: The buckling check is to be performed for all design load sets corresponding to the design loading conditions defined in Relevant Sections with the most unfavorable pressure combinations.

For each design load set, for all static and dynamic load cases, the lateral pressure is to be determined at the load calculation point defined in 3-2-A8/3.1.2(a), and is to be applied together with the hull girder stress combinations defined in Relevant Sections.

## 3.1.3 Assumptions for Equivalent Plate Panels

3.1.3(a) Longitudinal stiffening with varying plate thickness

In longitudinal stiffening arrangement, when the plate thickness varies over the width of a plate panel, the buckling check is to be performed for an equivalent plate panel width, combined with the smaller plate thickness, $t _ { 1 }$ . The width of this equivalent plate panel, $b _ { e q } ~ ,$ , in mm, is defined by the following formula:

$$
b _ {e q} = \ell_ {1} + \ell_ {2} \left(\frac {t _ {1}}{t _ {2}}\right) ^ {1. 5}
$$

where:

$\ell _ { 1 }$ = Width of the part of the plate panel with the smaller plate thickness, $t _ { 1 }$ , in mm, as defined in 3-2-A8/Figure 8.

$\ell _ { 2 }$ = Width of the part of the plate panel with the greater plate thickness, $t _ { 2 } ,$ in mm, as defined in 3-2-A8/Figure 8.

## 3.1.3(b) Transverse stiffening with varying plate thickness

In transverse stiffening arrangement, when an EPP is made with different thicknesses, the buckling check of the plate and stiffeners is to be made for each thickness considered constant on the EPP, the stresses and pressures being estimated for the EPP at the LCP.

## 3.1.3(c) Plate panel with different materials

When the plate panel is made of different materials, the minimum yield strength is to be used for the buckling assessment.

## 3.2 Buckling Criteria

## 3.2.1 Overall Stiffened Panel

3.2.1(a)

The buckling strength of overall stiffened panels is to satisfy the following criterion:

ηoverall ≤ ηall

where:

= Maximum overall buckling utilization factor as defined in 3-2-A8/5.2.1.

## 3.2.2 Plates

3.2.2(a)

The buckling strength of elementary plate panels is to satisfy the following criterion:

ηplate ≤ ηall

where:

= Maximum plate buckling utilization factor as defined in 3-2-A8/5.2.2 where SP-A model is to be used.

For the determination of of the vertically stiffened side shell plating of single side skin bulk carrier between hopper and topside tanks, the cases 12 and 16 of 3-2-A8/Table 5 corresponding to the shorter edge of the plate panel clamped are to be considered together with a mean stress and $\psi _ { y } = 1$

## 3.2.3 Stiffeners

3.2.3(a)

The buckling strength of stiffeners or of side frames of single side skin bulk carriers is to satisfy the following criterion:

ηstif fener ≤ Nall

where:

= Maximum stiffener buckling utilization factor as defined in 3-2-A8/5.2.3.

Notes:

1 This buckling check can only be fulfilled when the overall stiffened panel buckling check, as defined in 3-2-A8/3.2.1, is satisfied.

2 The buckling check of the stiffeners is only applicable to the stiffeners fitted along the long edge of the buckling panel.

## 3.2.4 Vertically Corrugated Longitudinal Bulkheads

The shear buckling strength of vertically corrugated longitudinal bulkheads is to satisfy the following criterion:

ηshear ≤ ηall

where:

= Maximum shear buckling utilization factor, defined as

$$
\eta_ {s h e a r} = \frac {\tau_ {b h d}}{\tau_ {c}}
$$

Tbhd = Shear stress, in N/mm<sup>2</sup>, in the bulkhead taken as the hull girder shear stress defined in Relevant Sections

$\tau _ { c }$ = Shear critical stress, in N/mm<sup>2</sup>, as defined in 3-2-A8/5.2.2(c).

## 3.2.5 Horizontally Corrugated Longitudinal Bulkheads

## 3.2.5(a)

Each corrugation unit within the extension of half flange, web and half flange (i.e. single corrugation as shown in grey in 3-2-A8/Figure 9) is to satisfy the following criterion:

Ncolumn $\leq$ Nall

where:

ηcolumn = Overall column buckling utilization factor, as defined in 3-2-A8/5.3.1.
